Parametrised Presentability over Orbital Categories
Kaif Hilman

Abstract
In this paper, we develop the notion of presentability in the parametrised homotopy theory framework of [ BDG+16 ] over orbital categories. We formulate and prove a characterisation of parametrised presentable categories in terms of its associated straightening. From this we deduce a parametrised adjoint functor theorem from the unparametrised version, prove various localisation results, and we record the interactions of the notion of presentability here with multiplicative matters. Such a theory is of interest for example in equivariant homotopy theory, and we will apply it in [ Hil22a ] to construct the category of parametrised noncommutative motives for equivariant algebraic K-theory.



1
Introduction

Parametrised homotopy theory is the study of higher categories fibred over a base
\infty
-category. This is a generalisation of the usual theory of higher categories, which can be viewed as the parametrised homotopy theory over a point. The advantage of this approach is that many structures can be cleanly encoded by the morphisms in the base
\infty
-category. For example, in the algebro-geometric world, various forms of pushforwards exist for various classes of scheme morphisms (see
[
BH21
]
for more details). Another example, which is the main motivation of this work for our applications in
[
Hil22a
]
, is that of genuine equivariant homotopy theory for a finite group
G
- here the base
\infty
-category would be
\mathcal{O}_{G}^{\mathrm{op}}
, the opposite of the
G
-orbit category. In this case, for subgroups
H\leq K\leq G
, important and fundamental constructions such as
indexed coproducts
,
indexed products
, and
indexed tensors

\coprod_{K/H}\quad\quad\quad\quad\prod_{K/H}\quad\quad\quad\quad\bigotimes_{K/H}

can be encoded by the morphisms in
\mathcal{O}_{G}^{\mathrm{op}}
. One framework in which to study this is the series of papers following
[
BDG+16
]
and the results in this paper should be viewed as a continuation of the vision from the aforementioned series - we refer the reader to them for more motivations and examples.

For an
\infty
-category to admit all small colimits and limits is a very desirable property as it means that many constructions can be done in it. However, this property entails that it has to be large enough and we might lose control of it due to size issues. Fortunately, there is a fix to this problem in the form of the very well-behaved class of
presentable

\infty
-categories: these are cocomplete
\infty
-categories that are “essentially generated” by a small subcategory. One of the most important features of presentable
\infty
-categories is the adjoint functor theorem which says that one can test whether or not a functor between presentables is right or left adjoint by checking that it preserves limits or colimits respectively. The
\infty
-categorical theory of presentability was developed by Lurie in
[
Lur09
, Chapter 5]
, generalising the classical 1-categorical notion of
locally presentable categories
.

The goal of this paper is to translate the above-mentioned theory of presentable
\infty
-categories to the parametrised setting and to understand the relationship between the notion of parametrised presentability and its unparametrised analogue in
[
Lur09
]
. As a signpost to the expert reader, we will always assume throughout this paper that the base category is orbital in the sense of
[
Nar17
]
. Besides that, we will adopt the convention in said paper of defining a
{\mathcal{T}}
-category, for a fixed based
\infty
-category
{\mathcal{T}}
, to be a cocartesian fibration over the
opposite
,
{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}
. This convention is geared towards equivariant homotopy theory as introduced in the motivation above where
T=\mathcal{O}_{G}
. Note that by the straightening-unstraightening equivalence of
[
Lur09
]
, a
{\mathcal{T}}
-category can equivalently be thought of as a functor
{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}\rightarrow\widehat{\mathrm{Cat}}_{\infty}
. The first main result we obtain is then the following characterisation of parametrised presentable
\infty
-categories.

Theorem A

(Straightening characterisation of parametrised presentables, full version in
6.1.2
)
.

Let
{\mathcal{C}}
be a
{\mathcal{T}}
-category. Then it is
{\mathcal{T}}
-presentable if and only if the associated straightening
C:{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}\rightarrow\widehat{\mathrm{Cat}}_{\infty}
factors through the non-full subcategory
\mathrm{Pr}^{\mathrm{L}}\subset\widehat{\mathrm{Cat}}_{\infty}
of presentable categories and left adjoint functors, and morevoer these functors themselves have left adjoints satisfying certain Beck-Chevalley conditions (
3.1.8
).

In the full version, we also give a complete parametrised analogue of the characterisations of presentable
\infty
-categories due to Lurie and Simpson (cf.
[
Lur09
, Thm. 5.5.1.1]
), which in particular shows that the notion defined in this paper is equivalent to the one defined in
[
Nar17
,
\lx@sectionsign 1.4
]
. While it is generally expected that the theory of
\infty
-cosmoi in
[
RV22
]
should absorb the statement and proof of the Lurie-Simpson-style characterisations of presentability, the value of the theorem above is in clarifying the relationship between the notion of presentability in the parametrised sense and in the unparametrised sense. Indeed, the description in
A
is a genuinely parametrised statement that is not seen in the unparametrised realm where
T=\ast
. One consequence of this is that we can easily deduce the parametrised adjoint functor theorem
from
the unparametrised version instead of repeating the same arguments in the parametrised setting.

Theorem B

(Parametrised adjoint functor theorem,
6.2.1
)
.

Let
F:{\mathcal{C}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{D}}
be a
{\mathcal{T}}
-functor between
{\mathcal{T}}
-presentable categories. Then:

1.

If
F
strongly preserves
{\mathcal{T}}
-colimits, then
F
admits a
{\mathcal{T}}
-right adjoint.

2.

If
F
strongly preserves
{\mathcal{T}}
-limits and is
{\mathcal{T}}
-accessible, then
F
admits a
{\mathcal{T}}
-left adjoint.

Another application of
A
is the construction of
presentable Dwyer-Kan localisations
,
6.3.7
. This is deduced essentially by performing fibrewise localisations, which are in turn furnished by
[
Lur09
]
. It is an extremely important construction, much like in the unparametrised world, and we will for example use it in
[
Hil22a
]
to understand the parametrised enhancement of the noncommutative motives of
[
BGT13
]
. Other highlights include the
localisation-cocompletions
construction in
6.4.2
, the idempotent-complete-presentables correspondence
6.5.4
, as well as studying the various interactions between presentability with multiplicative matters and functor categories in
Section

6.7
where, among other things, we prove a formula for the tensor product of parametrised presentable categories that was claimed in
[
Nar17
]
without proof.

We now comment on the methods and philosophy of this article. The approach taken here is an axiomatic one and is slightly different in flavour from the series of papers in
[
BDG+16
]
in that we freely pass between the viewpoint of parametrised
\infty
-categories as cocartesian fibrations and as
\infty
-category-valued functors via the straightening-unstraightening equivalence of Lurie. This allows us to work model-independently, ie. without thinking of our
\infty
-categories as simplicial sets. The point is that, as far as presentability and adjunctions are concerned, the foundations laid in
[
BDG+16a
,
BGN14
,
Sha23
,
Sha22
,
Nar17
]
are sufficient for us to make model-independent formulations and proofs via universal properties. Indeed, a recurring trick in this paper is to say that relevant universal properties guarantee the existence of certain functors, and then we can just check that certain diagrams of
\infty
-categories commute by virtue of the essential uniqueness of left/right adjoints.

Outline of paper.
In
Sections

2
,
3
and
4
we collect all the background materials, together with references, that will be needed for the rest of the paper. We hope that this establishes notational consistency and makes the paper as self-contained as possible. We have denoted by “recollections” those subsections which contain mostly only statements that have appeared in the literature. We recommend the reader to skim this section on first reading and refer to it as necessary. In
Section

5
we introduce the notions of
{\mathcal{T}}
-compactness and
{\mathcal{T}}
-idempotent-completeness. We then come to the heart of the paper in
Section

6
where we state and prove various basic results about parametrised presentable
\infty
-categories as enumerated above.

Conventions and assumptions.
This paper is written in the language of
\infty
-categories and so from now on we will drop the adjective
\infty
- and mean
\infty
-categories when we say categories. Moreover, throughout the paper the base category
{\mathcal{T}}
will be assumed to be
orbital
(cf. Definition
2.1.11
) unless stated otherwise. We will also use the notation
\mathrm{Cat}
for the category of small categories and
\widehat{\mathrm{Cat}}_{\infty}
for the category of large categories.

Related work.
Since the appearance of this article, Louis Martini and Sebastian Wolf have also independently produced many similar results in
[
MW22
]
using a different formalism of working internal to an
\infty
–topos. An important point of departure of this work from
[
MW22
]
is the the following: because this article is geared towards the applications we have in mind in
[
Hil22a
]
, our setup crucially interacts well with the notion of parametrised symmetric monoidal structures (a.k.a. multiplicative norms), which to the best of our knowledge, is not yet formulated in their formalism at the present moment. Moreover, this work has also been incorporated as Chapters 1 and 2 of the author’s PhD thesis
[
Hil22
]
.

Acknowledgements.
I am grateful to Jesper Grodal, Markus Land, and Maxime Ramzi for useful comments, sanity checks, and many hours of enlightening conversations. I would also like to acknowledge my debt to Fabian Hebestreit and Ferdinand Wagner whose joint notes
[
HW21
]
on a lecture series given by the former have taught me much about how to use higher category theory model-independently. Finally, I would like to thank Malte Leip for proofreading the various drafts of this article. This article is based on work done during the author’s PhD which was supported by the Danish
National Research Foundation through the Copenhagen Centre for Geometry and Topology
(DNRF151).

2
Preliminaries: general base categories

2.1
Recollections: basic objects and constructions

Recollections 2.1.1
.

For a category
{\mathcal{T}}
, there is Lurie’s straightening-unstraightening equivalence
\mathrm{coCart}({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}})\simeq\func({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Cat})
(cf. for example
[
HW21
, Thm. I.23]
). The category of
{\mathcal{T}}
–categories
is then defined simply as
\func({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Cat})
and we also write this as
\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
. We will always denote a
{\mathcal{T}}
–category with an underline
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
. Under the equivalence above, the datum of a
{\mathcal{T}}
–category is equivalent to the datum of a cocartesian fibration
p\colon\totalCategory(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\rightarrow{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}
, and a
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor is defined just to be a morphism of
{\mathcal{T}}
–categories
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
, is then equivalently a map of cocartesian fibrations
\totalCategory(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\rightarrow\totalCategory(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
over
{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}
. For an object
V\in{\mathcal{T}}
, we will write
{\mathcal{C}}_{V}
or
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{V}
for the fibre of
\totalCategory(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\rightarrow{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}
over
V
.

Remark 2.1.2
.

The product
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\times\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
in
\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
of two
{\mathcal{T}}
–categories
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
is given as the pullback
\totalCategory(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\times_{{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}}\totalCategory(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
in the cocartesian fibrations perspective. We will always denote with
\times
when we are viewing things as
{\mathcal{T}}
–categories and we reserve
\times_{{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}}
for when we are viewing things as total categories. In this way, there will be no confusion as to whether or not
\times_{{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}}
denotes a pullback in
\mathrm{Cat}_{T}
: this will never be the case.

Notation 2.1.3
.

Since
\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}=\func({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Cat})
is naturally even a 2–category, for
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
, we have the
category
of
{\mathcal{T}}
–functors from
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
to
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
: this we write as
\func_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
. Unstraightening, we obtain
\func_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})\simeq\func^{\mathrm{cocart}}(\totalCategory(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}),\totalCategory(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}))\times_{\func(\totalCategory(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}),{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}})}\{p\}
where
\func^{\mathrm{cocart}}
is the full subcategory of functors preserving
{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}
–cocartesian morphisms.

Example 2.1.4
.

We now give some basic examples of
{\mathcal{T}}
–categories to set notation.

•

(Fibrewise
{\mathcal{T}}
–categories) Let
K\in\mathrm{Cat}
. Write
\tconstant_{\mathcal{T}}(K)\in\mathrm{Cat}_{T}
for the constant
K
–valued diagram. In other words,
\totalCategory(\tconstant_{{\mathcal{T}}}(K))\simeq K\times{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}
.

•

We write
\underline{\ast}\coloneqq\tconstant_{\mathcal{T}}(\ast)
. This is clearly a final object in
\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}=\func({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Cat})
.

•

(Corepresentable
{\mathcal{T}}
–categories)
Let
V\in{\mathcal{T}}
. Then we can consider the left (and so cocartesian) fibration associated to the functor
\map_{{\mathcal{T}}}\colon{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}
and denote this
{\mathcal{T}}
–category by
\underline{V}
. Note that
\totalCategory(\underline{V})\simeq({\mathcal{T}}_{/V})^{\mathrm{op}}
. By corepresentability of
\underline{V}
, we have
\func_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{V},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\simeq{\mathcal{C}}_{V}
. To wit, for
K\in\mathrm{Cat}
, by
2.1.13
, we have

\begin{split}\map_{\mathrm{Cat}}\big(K,\func_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{V},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\big)&\simeq\map_{\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}}\big(\underline{V},\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\tconstant(K),\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\big)\\
&\simeq\map_{\mathrm{Cat}}(K,{\mathcal{C}}_{V})\end{split}

Definition 2.1.5
.

The category of
{\mathcal{T}}
–
objects of
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is defined to be
\func_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{\ast},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
.

Remark 2.1.6
.

If
{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}
has an initial object
T\in{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}
, then this means that the category of
{\mathcal{T}}
–objects in
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is just
{\mathcal{C}}_{T}
.

(Parametrised opposites)
.

{\mathcal{T}}
–category
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}

–opposite

Observation 2.1.8
.

Let
\underline{V}
be a corepresentable
{\mathcal{T}}
–category. Then

since the functor
(-)^{\mathrm{op}}\colon\mathrm{Cat}\rightarrow\mathrm{Cat}
restricts to the identity on
\mathcal{S}
.

Construction 2.1.9
.

The cone and cocone are functors
(-)^{\triangleleft},(-)^{\triangleright}\colon\mathrm{Cat}\rightarrow\mathrm{Cat}
which add a (co)cone point to a category. Applying
\func({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}},-)
to this functor yields the
{\mathcal{T}}
–cone
and
–cocone
functors
(-)^{\underline{\triangleleft}}
and
(-)^{\underline{\triangleright}}
respectively. We refer to
[
Sha23
]
for more on this.

Definition 2.1.10
.

A
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor is
{\mathcal{T}}
-fully faithful
(resp.
{\mathcal{T}}
-equivalence
) if it is so fibrewise. There is the expected characterisation of
{\mathcal{T}}
–fully faithfulness in terms of
{\mathcal{T}}
–mapping spaces, see
3.3.2
.

Definition 2.1.11
.

We say that the category
{\mathcal{T}}
is
orbital
if the finite coproduct cocompletion
\mathrm{Fin}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
admits finite pullbacks. Here, by finite coproduct cocompletion, we mean the full subcategory of the presheaf category
\func({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}},\mathcal{S})
spanned by finite coproduct of representables. We say that it is
atomic
if every retraction is an equivalence.

Notation 2.1.12

(Basechange)
.

As in
[
Nar17
]
, we will write

\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{\underline{V}}\coloneqq\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\times\underline{V}=\totalCategory(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\times_{{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}}\totalCategory(\underline{V})
for the basechanged parametrised category, which is now viewed as a
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
–category. The
(-)_{\underline{V}}
is a useful reminder that we have basechanged to
V
, and so for example we will often use the notation
\func_{\underline{V}}
to mean
\func_{{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}}
and
not

\func_{\totalCategory(\underline{V})}\simeq\func_{({\mathcal{T}}_{/V})^{\mathrm{op}}}
.

Construction 2.1.13

(Internal
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor category,
[
BDG+16a
,
\lx@sectionsign 9
]
)
.

For
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
, there is a
{\mathcal{T}}
–category
\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
such that

\func_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{\mathcal{E}},\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}))\simeq\func_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{\mathcal{E}}\times\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})

This is because
\func({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Cat})
is presentable and the endofunctor
-\times\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
has a right adjoint since it preserves colimits. In particular, by a Yoneda argument we get
\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{\ast},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})\simeq\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
. Moreover, plugging in
\underline{\mathcal{E}}=\underline{\ast}
we see that
{\mathcal{T}}
–objects of the internal
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor object are just
{\mathcal{T}}
–functors. Furthermore, the
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor categories basechange well in that

\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})_{\underline{V}}\simeq\underline{\func}_{\underline{V}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{\underline{V}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}_{\underline{V}})

so the fibre over
V\in{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}
is given by
\func_{\underline{V}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{\underline{V}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}_{\underline{V}}).
To wit, for any
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
–category
\underline{\mathcal{E}}
,

\begin{split}\map_{(\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}})_{/\underline{V}}}(\underline{\mathcal{E}},\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})_{\underline{V}})&\simeq\map_{\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}}(\underline{\mathcal{E}},\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}))\\
&\simeq\map_{(\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}})_{/\underline{V}}}(\underline{\mathcal{E}}\times\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}_{\underline{V}})\\
&\simeq\map_{(\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}})_{/\underline{V}}}(\underline{\mathcal{E}}\times_{\underline{V}}{\mathcal{C}}_{\underline{V}},{\mathcal{D}}_{\underline{V}})\\
&\simeq\map_{(\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}})_{/\underline{V}}}(\underline{\mathcal{E}},\underline{\func}_{\underline{V}}({\mathcal{C}}_{\underline{V}},{\mathcal{D}}_{\underline{V}}))\end{split}

Notation 2.1.14

(Parametrised cotensors)
.

Let
I
be a small unparametrised category. Then the adjunction
-\times I:\mathrm{Cat}\rightleftarrows\mathrm{Cat}:\func(I,-)
induces the adjunction

(-\times I)_{*}:\func({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Cat})\rightleftarrows\func({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Cat}):\func(I,-)_{*}

Under the identification
\func({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Cat})\simeq\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
where
\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
is the category of
{{\mathcal{T}}}
-categories, it is clear that
(-\times I)_{*}
corresponds to the
{{\mathcal{T}}}
-functor
\tconstant_{{\mathcal{T}}}(I)\times-
, whose right adjoint we know is
\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\tconstant_{{\mathcal{T}}}(I),-)
. Therefore
\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\tconstant_{{\mathcal{T}}}(I),-)
implements the
fibrewise functor construction
. We will introduce the notation
{\fibfunc}(I,-)
for
\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\tconstant_{{\mathcal{T}}}(I),-)
. This satisfies the following properties whose proofs are immediate.

1.

\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
is cotensored over
\mathrm{Cat}
in the sense that for any
{{\mathcal{T}}}
-categories
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
we have

\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},{\fibfunc}(I,\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}))\simeq{\fibfunc}(I,\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}))

2.

{\fibfunc}(I,-)
preserves
{{\mathcal{T}}}
-adjunctions.

to0.0pt{\hskip-0.19133pt\raisebox{0.46193pt}[0.0pt]{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{op}$}\hss}\mbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{op}$}}}}}}))\end{split}

Construction 2.1.16

(Cofree parametrisation,
[
Nar17
, Def. 1.10]
)
.

Let
{\mathcal{D}}
be a category. There is a
{\mathcal{T}}
–category
\cofree({\mathcal{D}})\colon{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}\rightarrow\mathrm{Cat}
classified by
V\mapsto\func(({\mathcal{T}}_{/V})^{\mathrm{op}},{\mathcal{D}})
. This has the following universal property: if
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
, then there is a natural equivalence

\func_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\cofree({\mathcal{D}}))\simeq\func(\totalCategory(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}),{\mathcal{D}})

of ordinary
\infty
-categories. This construction is of foundational importance and it allows us to define the following two fundamental
{\mathcal{T}}
–categories.

Notation 2.1.17
.

We will write
\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}\coloneqq\cofree_{T}(\mathrm{Cat})
for the
{\mathcal{T}}
–
category of
{\mathcal{T}}
–categories
; we write
\underline{\mathcal{S}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}\coloneqq\cofree_{T}(\mathcal{S})
for the
{\mathcal{T}}
–category of
{\mathcal{T}}
–spaces
.

Theorem 2.1.18

(Parametrised straightening-unstraightening,
[
BDG+16a
, Prop. 8.3]
)
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
. Then there are equivalences

\func_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}_{{\mathcal{T}}})\simeq\mathrm{coCart}(\totalCategory(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}))\quad\quad\func_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{\mathcal{S}}_{{\mathcal{T}}})\simeq\mathrm{Left}(\totalCategory(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}))

Proof.

This is an immediate consequence of the usual straightening-unstraightening and the universal property of
{\mathcal{T}}
–categories of
{\mathcal{T}}
–objects above. For example,

\func_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}_{{\mathcal{T}}})\simeq\func(\totalCategory(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}),\mathrm{Cat})\simeq\mathrm{coCart}(\totalCategory(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}))

and similarly for spaces.
∎

2.2
Parametrised adjunctions

{\mathcal{T}}
–adjunctions as introduced in
[
Sha23
]
is based on the
relative adjunctions
of
[
Lur17
]
.

Definition 2.2.1

(
[
Lur17
, Def. 7.3.2.2]
)
.

Suppose we have diagrams of categories
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{D}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{D}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{E}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{E}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}

Then we say that:

•

For the first diagram,
G
admits a
left adjoint

F

relative to

\mathcal{E}
if
G
admits a left adjoint
F
such that for every
C\in{\mathcal{C}}
,
q
sends the unit
\eta:C\rightarrow GFC
to an equivalence in
\mathcal{E}
(equivalently, if
q\eta:q\Rightarrow p\circ F
exhibits a commutation
p\circ F\simeq q
by
[
Lur17
, Prop. 7.3.2.1]
).

•

For the second diagram,
F
admits a
right adjoint

G

relative to

\mathcal{E}
if
F
admits a right adjoint
G
such that for every
D\in{\mathcal{D}}
,
p
maps the counit
\varepsilon:FGD\rightarrow D
to an equivalence in
\mathcal{E}
(equivalently if
p\varepsilon:q\circ G\Rightarrow p
exhibits
q\circ G\simeq p
by
[
Lur17
, Prop. 7.3.2.1]
).

Observe that when
\mathcal{E}\simeq\ast
, this specialises to the usual notion of adjunctions.

Remark 2.2.2
.

These two definitions are compatible. To see this, assume the first condition for example, ie. that
G
has a left adjoint
F
relative to
\mathcal{E}
. We need to see that
F
then admits a right adjoint
G
relative to
\mathcal{E}
in the sense of the second condition, ie. that
p
sends the counit
\varepsilon:FGD\rightarrow D
to an equivalence in
\mathcal{E}
. For this just consider the commutative diagram
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces qG}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces qGFG}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces pFG}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces qG}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q\eta_{G}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces qG\varepsilon}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p\varepsilon}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}

where the triangle is by the adjunction, and the square is by the natural equivalence
qG\simeq p
.

Definition 2.2.3
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
. Then a
{\mathcal{T}}
-adjunction

F:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightleftarrows\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}:G
is defined to be a relative adjunction such that
F,G
are
{\mathcal{T}}
–functors. A
{\mathcal{T}}
-Bousfield localisation
is a
{\mathcal{T}}
–adjunction where the
{\mathcal{T}}
–right adjoint is
{\mathcal{T}}
–fully faithful.

Proposition 2.2.4

(Stability of relative adjunctions under pullbacks,
[
Lur17
, Prop. 7.3.2.5]
)
.

Suppose we have a relative adjunction
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{D}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{E}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}

Then for any functor
\mathcal{E}^{\prime}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}
the diagram of pullbacks
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}}\times_{\mathcal{E}}\mathcal{E}^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{D}}\times_{\mathcal{E}}\mathcal{E}^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{E}^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}

is again a relative adjunction.

We now have the following criteria to obtain relative adjunctions - these are just modified from Lurie’s more general assumptions.

Proposition 2.2.5

(Criteria for relative adjunctions,
[
Lur17
, Prop. 7.3.2.6]
)
.

Suppose
p:{\mathcal{C}}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}
,
q:{\mathcal{D}}\rightarrow\mathcal{E}
are cocartesian fibrations. If we have a map of cocartesian fibrations
F
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{D}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{E}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}

Then:

(1)

F
admits a right adjoint
G
relative to
\mathcal{E}
if and only if for each
E\in\mathcal{E}
the map of fibres
F_{E}:{\mathcal{C}}_{E}\rightarrow{\mathcal{D}}_{E}
admits a right adjoint
G_{E}
. The right adjoint need no longer be a map of cocartesian fibrations.

(2)

F
admits a left adjoint
L
relative to
\mathcal{E}
if and only if for each
E\in\mathcal{E}
the map of fibres
F_{E}:{\mathcal{C}}_{E}\rightarrow{\mathcal{D}}_{E}
admits a left adjoint
L_{E}
and the canonical comparison maps (constructed in
[
Lur17
, Prop. 7.3.2.11]
)

Lf^{*}\rightarrow LFf^{*}L\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}f^{*}L

constructed from the fibrewise adjunction are equivalences - here
f^{*}
is the pushforward given by the cocartesian lift along some
f:E^{\prime}\rightarrow E
in
\mathcal{E}
. The relative left adjoint, if it exists, must necessarily be a map of cocartesian fibrations.

Proof.

We prove each in turn. To see (1), suppose
F
has an
\mathcal{E}
-right adjoint
G
. Then for each
e\in\mathcal{E}
the inclusion
\{e\}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{E}
induces a pullback relative adjunction over the point
\{e\}
by
2.2.4
, and so we get the statement on fibres. Conversely, suppose we have fibrewise right adjoints. To construct an
\mathcal{E}
-right adjoint
G
, since adjunctions can be constructed objectwise by the unparametrised version of
3.3.9
below, we need to show that for each
e\in\mathcal{E}
and
d\in{\mathcal{D}}_{e}
, there is a
Gd\in{\mathcal{C}}_{e}
and a map
\varepsilon:FGd\rightarrow d
such that:

(a)

For every
c\in{\mathcal{C}}
the following composition is an equivalence

\map_{{\mathcal{C}}}(c,Gd)\xrightarrow{F}\map_{{\mathcal{D}}}(Fc,FGd)\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}\map_{{\mathcal{D}}}(Fc,d)

(b)

The morphism
p\varepsilon:pFGd\rightarrow pd
is an equivalence in
\mathcal{E}
.

We can just define
Gd\coloneqq G_{e}(d)\in{\mathcal{C}}_{e}
given by the fibrewise right adjoint and let
\varepsilon:FGd\rightarrow d
be the fibrewise counit. Since these are fibrewise, point (b) is automatic. To see point (a), let
c\in{\mathcal{C}}_{e^{\prime}}
for some
e^{\prime}\in\mathcal{E}
. Since the mapping space in the total category of cocartesian fibrations are just disjoint unions over the components lying under
\map_{{\mathcal{C}}}(c,Gd)
, we can work over some
f\in\map_{\mathcal{E}}(e^{\prime},e)
. Consider
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\map^{f}_{{\mathcal{C}}}(c,Gd)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\map_{{\mathcal{D}}_{e}}(f^{*}Fc,d)\simeq\map_{{\mathcal{D}}}^{f}(Fc,d)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\map_{{\mathcal{C}}_{e}}(f^{*}c,Gd)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\map_{{\mathcal{D}}_{e}}(f^{*}Fc,FGd)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varepsilon}

where we have used also that
F
was a map of cocartesian fibrations so that
f^{*}F\simeq Ff^{*}
and that the diagonal map is an equivalence since we had a fibrewise adjunction
F_{e}\dashv G_{e}
by hypothesis. This completes the proof of part (1).

For case (2), to see the cocartesianness of a relative left adjoint
L
, note

\begin{split}\map_{{\mathcal{C}}}(Lf^{*}d,c)\simeq\map_{{\mathcal{D}}}(f^{*}d,Fc)&\simeq\map^{f}_{{\mathcal{D}}}(d,Fc)\\
&\simeq\map_{{\mathcal{C}}}^{f}(Ld,c)\simeq\map_{{\mathcal{C}}}(f^{*}Ld,c)\end{split}

The proof for right adjoints in (1) go through in this case but now we use
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\map_{{\mathcal{C}}}^{f}(Ld,c)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\map_{{\mathcal{D}}_{E}}(f^{*}d,Fc)\simeq\map_{{\mathcal{D}}}^{f}(d,Fc)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\map_{{\mathcal{C}}_{E}}(f^{*}Ld,c)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\map_{{\mathcal{C}}_{E}}(Lf^{*}d,c)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}

and so the technical condition in the statement says that there is a canonical map inducing the bottom map in the square which must necessarily be an equivalence.
∎

Remark 2.2.6
.

One might object to the notation we have adopted for the pushforward being
f^{*}
instead of
f_{!}
. This convention is standard in the framework of
[
BDG+16
]
because the latter notation is reserved for the
left adjoint
of
f^{*}
(the so-called
{\mathcal{T}}
–coproducts) that will be recalled later.

Corollary 2.2.7

(Fibrewise criteria for
{\mathcal{T}}
–adjunctions)
.

Let
F:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
be a
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor. Then it admits a
{\mathcal{T}}
–right adjoint if and only if it has fibrewise right adjoints
G_{V}
for all
V\in{\mathcal{T}}
and
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}}_{W}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{D}}_{W}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}}_{V}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{D}}_{V}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G_{W}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G_{V}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}}

commutes for all
f:W\rightarrow V
in
{\mathcal{T}}
. Similarly for left
{\mathcal{T}}
–adjoints.

Proof.

The commuting square ensures that the relative right adjoint is a
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor.
∎

Proposition 2.2.8

(Criteria for
{\mathcal{T}}
–Bousfield localisations, “
[
Lur09
, Prop. 5.2.7.4]
”)
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
and
L:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
a
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor equipped with a fibrewise natural transformation
\eta:\mathrm{id}\Rightarrow L
. Let
j:L\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\subseteq\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
be the inclusion of the
{\mathcal{T}}
–full subcategory spanned by the image of
L
. Suppose the transformations
L\eta,\eta_{L}:L\Longrightarrow L\circ L
are equivalences. Then the pair
(L,j)
constitutes a
{\mathcal{T}}
–Bousfield localisation with unit
\eta
.

Proof.

We want to apply
2.2.7
. Since we are already provided with the fact that
L
was a
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor, all that is left to show is that it is fibrewise left adjoint to the inclusion
L\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\subseteq\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
. But this is guaranteed by
[
Lur09
, Prop. 5.2.7.4]
, and so we are done.
∎

Finally, we show that parametrised adjunctions have the expected internal characterisation in terms of the parametrised mapping spaces recalled in
3.3.1
.

Lemma 2.2.9

(Mapping space characterisation of
{\mathcal{T}}
–adjunctions)
.

Let
F:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\leftrightarrows\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}:G
be a pair of
{\mathcal{T}}
–functors. Then there is a
{\mathcal{T}}
–adjunction
F\dashv G
if and only if we have a natural equivalence

\mathchoice{\mbox{\uline{\phantom{$\displaystyle\map$}}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip 0.0pt\raisebox{0.5pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip 0.46193pt\raisebox{0.19133pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip 0.5pt\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip 0.46193pt\raisebox{-0.19133pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip 0.35355pt\raisebox{-0.35355pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip to0.0pt{\hskip-0.19133pt\raisebox{-0.46193pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip-0.35355pt\raisebox{-0.35355pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip-0.46193pt\raisebox{-0.19133pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip-0.5pt\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip-0.46193pt\raisebox{0.19133pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip-0.35355pt\raisebox{0.35355pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip-0.19133pt\raisebox{0.46193pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\mbox{$\displaystyle\map$}}}}{\mbox{\uline{\phantom{$\textstyle\map$}}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\hbox Proof.

The if direction is clear: since
F
and
G
were already
{\mathcal{T}}
–functors, by
2.2.7
the only thing left to do is to show fibrewise adjunction, and this is easily implied by the equivalence which supplies the unit and counits. For the only if direction, by definition of a relative adjunction, we have a fibrewise natural transformation
\eta:\mathrm{id}_{{\mathcal{C}}}\Rightarrow GF
(ie. a morphism in
\func_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
) and so we obtain a natural comparison

3
Preliminaries: orbital base categories

Some of the notions here still make sense for general
{\mathcal{T}}
, but we want orbitality in order to make formulations involving Beck-Chevalley conditions. Hence, from now on, we assume that
{\mathcal{T}}
is orbital.

3.1
Recollections: colimits and Kan extensions

Definition 3.1.1
.

Let
\underline{K}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
and
q\colon\underline{K}\rightarrow\underline{\ast}
be the unique map. Then precomposition induces the
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor

q^{*}:\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\simeq\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{\ast},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})\longrightarrow\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{K},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
. The
{\mathcal{T}}
–left adjoint
q_{!}
, if it exists, is called the
\underline{K}
–indexed
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimit
, and similarly for
T-limits

q_{*}
.

Example 3.1.2
.

Here are some special and important classes of these:

•

A
{\mathcal{T}}
–(co)limit indexed by
\tconstant_{\mathcal{T}}(K)
for some ordinary
\infty
–category
K
is called a
fibrewise

{\mathcal{T}}
-(co)limit.

•

A
{\mathcal{T}}
–(co)limit indexed by a corepresentable
{\mathcal{T}}
–category
\underline{V}
(cf.
•
‣
Example

2.1.4
) of some
V\in{\mathcal{T}}
is called the
T-(co)product.

Definition 3.1.3

(
[
Sha23
, Def. 11.2]
)
.

Let
F:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
be a
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor.

•

We say that it
preserves

{\mathcal{T}}
-colimits
if for all
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimit diagrams
\overline{d}:K^{\underline{\triangleright}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
, the post-composed diagram
F\circ\overline{d}:K^{\underline{\triangleright}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
is a
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimit. Similarly for
{\mathcal{T}}
–limits.

•

We say that
F

strongly preserves

{\mathcal{T}}
-colimits
if for all
V\in{\mathcal{T}}
,
F_{\underline{V}}:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{\underline{V}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}_{\underline{V}}
preserves
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
–colimits. Similarly for
{\mathcal{T}}
–limits.

Warning 3.1.4

(
[
Sha23
, Rmk. 5.14]
)
.

Note that being
{\mathcal{T}}
–cocomplete is much stronger than just admitting all
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits. This is because admitting all
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits just means that any
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
–diagram
\underline{K}_{\underline{V}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{\underline{V}}
pulled back from a
{\mathcal{T}}
–diagram
\underline{K}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
admits a
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
–colimit. However not every
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
–diagram is pulled back as such. We will elaborate on the distinction of these definitions in the next subsection. In this document, we will never consider preservations, but only strong preservations.

Definition 3.1.5

(
[
Sha23
, Def. 5.13]
)
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
. Then we say
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is
{\mathcal{T}}
–(co)complete
if for all
V\in{\mathcal{T}}
and
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
–diagram
p:\underline{K}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{\underline{V}}
with
\underline{K}
small,
p
admits a
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
–(co)limit.

Terminology 3.1.6
.

When we want to specify particular kinds of parametrised (co)limits that a
{\mathcal{T}}
–category admits, it is convenient to use the following terminology: for
\mathcal{K}=\{\mathcal{K}_{V}\}_{V\in{\mathcal{T}}}
some collection of diagrams varying over
V\in{\mathcal{T}}
, we say that
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}

strongly admits

\mathcal{K}
–(co)limits if for all
V\in{\mathcal{T}}
,
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{\underline{V}}
admits
\underline{K}
–colimits for all
\underline{K}\in\mathcal{K}_{V}
. Examples include:

•

\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
strongly admits all
{\mathcal{T}}
–(co)limits means that it is
{\mathcal{T}}
–(co)cocomplete,

•

Let
\kappa
be a regular cardinal. We say that
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
strongly admits
\kappa
–small
{\mathcal{T}}
–(co)products to mean that it has
{\mathcal{T}}
–(co)limits for any diagram indexed over
\coprod_{a\in A}\underline{V}_{a}
where
A
is a
\kappa
–small set. Hence, strongly admitting finite
{\mathcal{T}}
–(co)products means admitting finite fibrewise (co)products and (co)limits for all corepresentable diagrams
\underline{V}
.

Lemma 3.1.7

(Decomposition of indexed coproducts)
.

Let
R_{a},V\in{\mathcal{T}}
and
\coprod_{a}f_{a}:\coprod_{a}R_{a}\rightarrow V
be a map where the coproduct is not necessarily finite. Suppose
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
strongly admits finite
{\mathcal{T}}
–coproducts and arbitrary fibrewise coproducts. Then
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
admits
\coprod_{a}f_{a}
-coproducts and this is computed by composing fibrewise
{\mathcal{T}}
–coproduct
\coprod_{a}
with the individual indexed
{\mathcal{T}}
–coproducts.

Proof.

We will in fact show that we have
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
–adjunctions

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\func}_{\underline{V}}(\coprod_{a}\underline{R_{a}},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{\underline{V}})=\prod_{a}\underline{\func}_{\underline{V}}(\underline{R_{a}},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{\underline{V}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\prod_{a}\underline{\func}_{\underline{V}}(\underline{V},{\mathcal{C}}_{\underline{V}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\func}_{\underline{V}}(\underline{V},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{\underline{V}})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\prod_{a}(f_{a})_{!}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod_{a}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\prod_{a}(f_{a})^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Delta}

That these
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
–adjunctions exist is by our hypotheses, and all that is left to do is check that
\prod_{a}(f_{a})^{*}\circ\Delta\simeq(\coprod_{a}f_{a})^{*}
. But this is also clear since we have the commuting diagram
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod_{a}\underline{R_{a}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{V}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod_{a}\underline{V}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod_{a}f_{a}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{a}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod_{a}\mathrm{id}_{V}}

Applying
(-)^{*}
to this triangle completes the proof.
∎

Terminology 3.1.8

(Beck-Chevalley conditions)
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
that admits finite fibrewise coproducts (resp. products) and such that for each
f:W\rightarrow V
in
{\mathcal{T}}
,
f^{*}:{\mathcal{C}}_{V}\rightarrow{\mathcal{C}}_{W}
admits a left adjoint
f_{!}
(resp. right adjoint
f_{*}
). We say that
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
satisfies the
left Beck-Chevalley condition
(resp.
right Beck-Chevalley condition
) if for every pair of morphisms
f:W\rightarrow V
and
g:Y\rightarrow V
in
{\mathcal{T}}
: in the pullback (whose orbital decomposition exists by orbitality of
{\mathcal{T}}
)
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod_{a}R_{a}=Y\times_{V}W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V}

\lrcorner

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod_{a}f_{a}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod_{a}g_{a}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

the canonical basechange transformation

\coprod_{a}g_{a_{!}}f^{*}_{a}\Longrightarrow f^{*}g_{!}\quad\Big(\text{resp. }f^{*}g_{*}\Longrightarrow\prod_{a}g_{a_{*}}f^{*}_{a}\Big)

is an equivalence.

Here is an omnibus of results due to Jay Shah.

Theorem 3.1.9

(
[
Sha23
, 5.5-5.12 and
\lx@sectionsign 12
]

)
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
. Then:

(1)

(Fibrewise criterion)
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
strongly admits
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits indexed by
\tconstant_{\mathcal{T}}(K)
if and only if for every
V\in{\mathcal{T}}
the fibre
{\mathcal{C}}_{V}
has all colimits indexed by
K
and for every morphism
f:W\rightarrow V
in
{\mathcal{T}}
the cocartesian lift
f^{*}:{\mathcal{C}}_{V}\rightarrow{\mathcal{C}}_{W}
preserves colimits indexed by
K
. A cocone diagram
\overline{p}:\tconstant_{{\mathcal{T}}}(K)^{\underline{\triangleright}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is a
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimit if and only if it is so fibrewise.

(1)

(T-coproducts criteria)
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
strongly admits finite
{\mathcal{T}}
–coproducts if and only if we have:

(a)

For every
W\in{\mathcal{T}}
the fibre
{\mathcal{C}}_{W}
has all finite coproducts and for every
f:W\rightarrow V
in
{\mathcal{T}}
the map
f^{*}:{\mathcal{C}}_{V}\rightarrow{\mathcal{C}}_{W}
preserves finite coproducts,

(b)

{\mathcal{C}}
satisfies the left Beck-Chevalley condition (cf.
3.1.8
).

(3)

(Decomposition principle)
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is
{\mathcal{T}}
–cocomplete if and only if it has all fibrewise colimits and strongly admits finite
{\mathcal{T}}
–coproducts.

Similar statements hold for
{\mathcal{T}}
–limits, and the right adjoint to
f^{*}
will be denoted
f_{*}
.

Theorem 3.1.10

(Omnibus
{\mathcal{T}}
–adjunctions,
[
Sha23
,
\lx@sectionsign 8
]
)
.

Let
F:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightleftarrows\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}:G
be a
{\mathcal{T}}
–adjunction and
\underline{I}
be a
{\mathcal{T}}
–category. Then:

(1)

We get adjunctions

F_{*}\colon\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\rightleftarrows\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}):G_{*}
,
G^{*}\colon\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{I})\rightleftarrows\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}},\underline{I}):F^{*}
. By
2.2.7
this implies ordinary adjunctions when we replace
\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
by
\func_{{\mathcal{T}}}
.

(2)

F
strongly preserves
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits and
G
strongly preserves
{\mathcal{T}}
–limits.

Proof.

In
[
Sha23
, Cor. 8.9]
, part (2) was stated only as ordinary preservation, not strong preservation. But then strong preservation was implicit since relative adjunctions are stable under pullbacks by
2.2.4
, and the statement in
[
Sha23
]
also holds after pulling back to
-\times\underline{V}
for all
V\in{\mathcal{T}}
.
∎

Proposition 3.1.11

(
{\mathcal{T}}
–cocompleteness of Bousfield local subcategories)
.

If
L:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightleftarrows\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}:j
is a
{\mathcal{T}}
–Bousfield localisation where
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is
{\mathcal{T}}
–cocomplete, then
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
is too and
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits in
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
is computed as
L
applied to the
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimit computed in
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
.

Proof.

This is an immediate consequence of
2.2.9
.
∎

Proposition 3.1.12

(
{\mathcal{T}}
–(co)limits of functor categories is pointwise)
.

Let
\underline{K},\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
be
{\mathcal{T}}
–categories. Suppose
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
strongly admits
\underline{K}
–indexed diagrams. Then so does
\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
and the parametrised (co)limits are inherited from that of
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
.

Proof.

This is a direct consequence of the adjunction

(\underline{\mathop{colim}\displaylimits}_{\underline{K}})_{*}:\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{K},\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}))\simeq\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{I},\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{K},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}))\rightleftarrows\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}):\operatorname{const}
for
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits. The other case is similar.
∎

Definition 3.1.13

(
{\mathcal{T}}
–Kan extensions)
.

Let
j:\underline{I}\rightarrow\underline{K}
be a
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor. If

j^{*}:\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{K},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})\longrightarrow\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
has a
{\mathcal{T}}
–left adjoint, then we denote it by
j_{!}
and call it the
T-left Kan extension
. Similarly for
{\mathcal{T}}
–right Kan extensions.

Proposition 3.1.14

(Fully faithful
{\mathcal{T}}
–Kan extensions,
[
Sha23
, Prop. 10.6]
)
.

Let
i:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\hookrightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
be a
{\mathcal{T}}
–fully faithful functor and
F:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathcal{E}}
be another
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor. If the
{\mathcal{T}}
–left Kan extension
i_{!}F
exists, then the adjunction unit
F\Rightarrow i^{*}i_{!}F\colon\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathcal{E}}
is an equivalence.

Theorem 3.1.15

(Omnibus
{\mathcal{T}}
–Kan extensions,
[
Sha23
, Thm. 10.5]
)
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
be
{\mathcal{T}}
–cocomplete. Then for every
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor of small
{\mathcal{T}}
–categories
f:\underline{I}\rightarrow\underline{K}
, the
{\mathcal{T}}
–left Kan extension
f_{!}:\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\longrightarrow\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{K},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
exists.

3.2
Strong preservation of
{\mathcal{T}}
-colimits

We now explain in more detail the notion of strong preservation. In particular, the reader may find
3.2.2
to be a convenient alternative description, and we will have many uses of it in the coming sections.

Observation 3.2.1

(Strong preservations vs preservations)
.

Here are some comments for the distinction.
3.2.2
will then characterise strong preservations more concretely.

(1)

Recall
3.1.4
that admitting
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits is weaker than being
{\mathcal{T}}
–cocomplete. In the proof of the Lurie-Simpson characterisation
6.1.2
, we will see that we really need
{\mathcal{T}}
–cocompleteness via
3.2.2
.

(2)

However,
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
admitting
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits indexed by
p:\underline{K}\rightarrow{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}
does imply
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{\underline{V}}
admits
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
–colimits indexed by
\underline{K}_{\underline{V}}
. This is because the adjunction
p_{!}\colon\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{K},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\rightleftarrows\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{\ast},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}):p^{*}
pulls back to the
p_{!}\colon\underline{\func}_{\underline{V}}(\underline{K}_{\underline{V}},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{\underline{V}})\rightleftarrows\underline{\func}_{\underline{V}}({\underline{V}},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{\underline{V}}):p^{*}
adjunction by
2.2.4
. We have also used that functor
{\mathcal{T}}
–categories basechange well by
2.1.13
.

(3)

Strongly preserving fibrewise
{\mathcal{T}}
–(co)limits is equivalent to preserving these (co)limits on each fibre since by
3.1.9
fibrewise (co)limits are constructed fibrewise.

The following result was also recorded in the recent
[
Sha22
, Thm. 8.6]
.

Proposition 3.2.2

(Characterisation of strong preservations)
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
be
{\mathcal{T}}
–cocomplete categories and
F:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
a
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor. Then
F
strongly preserves
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits if and only if it preserves colimits in each fibre and for all
f:W\rightarrow V
in
{\mathcal{T}}
, the following square commutes (and similarly for
{\mathcal{T}}
–limits)
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}}_{W}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}}_{V}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{D}}_{W}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{D}}_{V}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{!}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F_{W}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F_{V}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{!}}

Proof.

To see the only if direction, that
F
preserves colimits in each fibre is clear since
F
in particular preserves fibrewise
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits. Now for
f:W\rightarrow V
, we basechange to
\underline{V}
. Since
F
strongly preserves
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits, we get commutative squares
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\func}_{\underline{V}}(\underline{W},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\times\underline{V})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\func}_{\underline{V}}(\underline{V},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\times\underline{V})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\func}_{\underline{V}}(\underline{W},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\times\underline{V})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\func}_{\underline{V}}(\underline{V},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\times\underline{V})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{!}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(F_{\underline{V}})_{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(F_{\underline{V}})_{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{!}}

Taking global sections by using that
\func_{\underline{V}}(\underline{W},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\times\underline{V})\simeq\func_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{W},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\simeq{\mathcal{C}}_{W}
from
•
‣
Example

2.1.4
, we get the desired square.

For the if direction, we know by
3.1.9
that all
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits can be decomposed as fibrewise
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits and indexed
{\mathcal{T}}
–coproducts, and so if we show strong preservation of these we would be done. By
3.2.1
(3) strong preservation of fibrewise
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits is the same as preserving colimits in each fibre, so this case is covered. Since arbitrary indexed
{\mathcal{T}}
–coproducts are just compositions of orbital
{\mathcal{T}}
–coproducts and arbitrary fibrewise coproducts by
3.1.7
, we need only show for orbital
{\mathcal{T}}
–coproducts, so let
f:W\rightarrow V
be a morphism in
{\mathcal{T}}
. We need to show that the canonical comparison in
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\func}_{\underline{V}}(\underline{W},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\times\underline{V})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\func}_{\underline{V}}(\underline{V},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\times\underline{V})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\func}_{\underline{V}}(\underline{W},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\times\underline{V})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\func}_{\underline{V}}(\underline{V},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\times\underline{V})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{!}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(F_{\underline{V}})_{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(F_{\underline{V}})_{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{!}}

is a natural equivalence. Since equivalences is by definition a fibrewise notion, we can check this on each fibre. So let
\varphi:Y\rightarrow V
be in
{\mathcal{T}}
, and consider the pullback
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod_{a}R_{a}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod f_{a}}

\lrcorner

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod\varphi_{a}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

by orbitality of
{\mathcal{T}}
. We need to show that
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\func}_{\underline{V}}(\underline{W},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\times\underline{V})_{Y}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\func}_{\underline{V}}(\underline{V},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\times\underline{V})_{Y}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\func}_{\underline{V}}(\underline{W},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\times\underline{V})_{Y}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\func}_{\underline{V}}(\underline{V},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\times\underline{V})_{Y}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{!}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(F_{\underline{V}})_{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(F_{\underline{V}})_{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{!}}

commutes. But then by the universal property of the internal functor
{\mathcal{T}}
–categories from
2.1.13
, this is the same as
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\func}_{\underline{Y}}(\coprod_{a}\underline{R_{a}},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\times\underline{Y})\simeq{\func}_{\underline{Y}}(\underline{W}\times_{\underline{V}}\underline{Y},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\times\underline{Y})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\func}_{\underline{Y}}(\underline{Y},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\times\underline{Y})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\func}_{\underline{Y}}(\coprod_{a}\underline{R_{a}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\times\underline{Y})\simeq{\func}_{\underline{Y}}(\underline{W}\times_{\underline{V}}\underline{Y},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\times\underline{Y})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\func}_{\underline{Y}}(\underline{Y},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\times\underline{Y})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{!}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(F_{\underline{Y}})_{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(F_{\underline{Y}})_{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{!}}

and this is in turn
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\prod_{a}{\mathcal{C}}_{R_{a}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}}_{Y}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\prod_{a}{\mathcal{D}}_{R_{a}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{D}}_{Y}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod(f_{a})_{!}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\prod F_{a}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F_{V}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod(f_{a})_{!}}

which commutes by hypothesis together with that
F
commutes with fibrewise
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits (and so in particular finite fibrewise coproducts). This finishes the proof of the result.
∎

{\mathcal{T}}
–fully faithful. On the other hand, by the universal property of the

Theorem 3.3.4

(Continuity of
{\mathcal{T}}
–Yoneda,
[
Sha23
, Cor. 11.10]
)
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
. The
{\mathcal{T}}
–yoneda embedding
j:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
strongly preserves and detects
{\mathcal{T}}
–limits.

Theorem 3.3.6

(
{\mathcal{T}}
–Yoneda density,
[
Sha23
, Lem. 11.1]
)
.

Let
j:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\hookrightarrow\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
be the
{\mathcal{T}}
–yoneda embedding. Then
\mathrm{id}_{\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})}\simeq j_{!}j
, that is, everything in the
{\mathcal{T}}
–presheaf is a
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimit of representables.

Theorem 3.3.7

(Universal property of
{\mathcal{T}}
–presheaves,
[
Sha23
, Thm. 11.5]
)
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
and suppose
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
is
{\mathcal{T}}
–cocomplete. Then the precompositions

j^{*}:\func_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{L}(\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}),\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})\longrightarrow\func_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
and
j^{*}:\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{L}(\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}),\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})\longrightarrow\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})

are equivalences with the inverse given by left Kan extensions. Here
\func_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{L}
means those functors which strongly preserve
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits (cf.
3.3.10
).

We learnt of the following useful procedure from Fabian Hebestreit.

Definition 3.3.8

(Adjoint objects)
.

Let
R:\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
be a
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor. Let
x\in\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
and
y\in\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
and
\eta:x\rightarrow R(y)
. We say that
\eta

witnesses
y
as a left adjoint object to
x
under
R

is an equivalence of
{\mathcal{T}}
–functors
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathcal{S}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
.

The following observation, due to Lurie, is quite surprising for
\infty
-categories: adjunctions can be constructed objectwise, ie. to check that we have an adjunction, it is enough to construct a left adjoint object for each object.

Proposition 3.3.9

(Pointwise construction of adjunctions)
.

R:\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
admits a left adjoint
L:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
if and only if all objects in
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
admits a left adjoint object. More generally, writing
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{R}
for the full subcategory of objects admitting left adjoint objects, we obtain a
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor
L:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{R}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
that is
{\mathcal{T}}
–left adjoint to the restriction of
R:\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
to the subcategory of
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
landing in
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}_{R}
.

Proof.

{\mathcal{T}}
–Yoneda lemma to help us assemble the various left adjoint objects into a coherent
{\mathcal{T}}

Notation 3.3.10
.

We write
\underline{\rfunc}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
(resp.
\underline{\lfunc}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
) for the
{\mathcal{T}}
–full subcategories in
\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
of
{\mathcal{T}}
–right adjoint functors (resp.
{\mathcal{T}}
–left adjoint functors). This is distinguished from the notations
\underline{\func}^{R}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
(resp.
\underline{\func}^{L}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
) by which we mean the
{\mathcal{T}}
–full subcategories in
\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
of strongly
{\mathcal{T}}
–limit-preserving functors (resp. strongly
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimit-preserving functors).

Proposition 3.3.11

(“
[
Lur09
, Prop. 5.2.6.2]
”)
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
. Then there is a canonical equivalence

3.4
(Full) faithfulness

In this subsection we provide the parametrised analogue of the Lurie-Thomason formula for limits in categories,
3.4.2
, as well as show that parametrised functor categories preserve (fully) faithfulness in
3.4.6
.

Notation 3.4.1
.

For
p:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{I}
a
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor which is also a cocartesian fibration, we will write
\underline{\Gamma}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\mathrm{cocart}}(p)
for the
{\mathcal{T}}
–category of cocartesian sections of
p
. In other words, it is the
{\mathcal{T}}
–category
\underline{\func}^{\mathrm{cocart}}_{T}(\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\times_{\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{I},\underline{I})}\underline{\ast}
where
\underline{\func}^{\mathrm{cocart}}_{T}(\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
means the full
{\mathcal{T}}
–subcategory of those that parametrised functors that preserve cocartesian morphisms over
\underline{I}
, and the
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor
\underline{\ast}\rightarrow\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{I},\underline{I})
is the section corresponding to the identity on
\underline{I}
.

The following proof is just a parametrisation of the unparametrised proof that we learnt from
[
HW21
, Prop. I.36]
.

Theorem 3.4.2

(Lurie-Thomason formula)
.

Given a
{\mathcal{T}}
–diagram
F:\underline{I}\rightarrow\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
, we get

\underline{\lim}_{\underline{I}}F\simeq\underline{\Gamma}_{T}^{\underline{I}\mathrm{-cocart}}(\mathrm{UnStr}^{\mathrm{cocart}}(F))

In particular, if it factors through
F:{\underline{I}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathcal{S}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
, then we have
\underline{\lim}_{\underline{I}}F\simeq\underline{\Gamma}_{T}(\mathrm{UnStr}^{\mathrm{cocart}}(F))
.

Proof.

Let
d:{\underline{I}}\rightarrow\underline{\ast}
be the unique map. Since
\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
has all
{\mathcal{T}}
–limits, we know abstractly that we have the
{\mathcal{T}}
–right adjoint

d^{*}:\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}\rightleftarrows\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}({\underline{I}},\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}):d_{*}=:\underline{\lim}_{{\mathcal{T}}}

so now we just need to understand the fibrewise right adjoint formula (by virtue of
2.2.7
). Without loss of generality, we work with global sections and we want to describe the right adjoint in

d^{*}:\func({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}},{\mathrm{Cat}})\rightleftarrows{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}({\underline{I}},\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}_{{\mathcal{T}}})\simeq\func(\totalCategory({\underline{I}}),\mathrm{Cat}):d_{*}

We can now identify
d^{*}
concretely via the straightening-unstraightening equivalence to get

d^{*}\colon\mathrm{coCart}({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}})\rightarrow\mathrm{coCart}(\totalCategory({\underline{I}}))
given by

\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\mapsto\big(\pi_{{\mathcal{C}}}:\totalCategory(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\times_{{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}}\totalCategory({\underline{I}})\rightarrow\totalCategory({\underline{I}})\big)

Let
(p:\mathcal{E}_{F}\rightarrow\totalCategory({\underline{I}}))\coloneqq\mathrm{UnStr}^{\mathrm{coCart}}(F)
be the cocartesian fibration associated to
F:\totalCategory({\underline{I}})\rightarrow\mathrm{Cat}
. We need to show that
\underline{\Gamma}_{T}^{\underline{I}\mathrm{-cocart}}(p)
satisfies a natural equivalence

\map_{\mathrm{coCart}(\totalCategory({\underline{I}}))}(\pi_{{\mathcal{C}}},p)\simeq\map_{\mathrm{coCart}({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}})}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{\Gamma}_{T}^{\underline{I}\mathrm{-cocart}}(p))

for all
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathrm{coCart}({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}})
. First of all, by definition we have the pullback

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\map_{\mathrm{coCart}({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}})_{/\totalCategory({\underline{I}})}}(\pi_{{\mathcal{C}}},p)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\map_{\mathrm{coCart}({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}})}(\totalCategory(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\times_{{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}}\totalCategory({\underline{I}}),\mathcal{E}_{F})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ast}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\map_{\mathrm{coCart}({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}})}(\totalCategory(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\times_{{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}}\totalCategory({\underline{I}}),\totalCategory({\underline{I}}))}

\lrcorner

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{{\mathcal{C}}}}

which by currying is the same as the pullback
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\map_{\mathrm{coCart}({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}})_{/\totalCategory({\underline{I}})}}(\pi_{{\mathcal{C}}},p)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\map_{\mathrm{coCart}({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}})}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}({\underline{I}},\mathcal{E}_{F}))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ast}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\map_{\mathrm{coCart}({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}})}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}({\underline{I}},{\underline{I}}))}

\lrcorner

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}_{\underline{I}}}

Now recall that
\map_{\mathrm{coCart}(\totalCategory({\underline{I}}))}(\pi_{{\mathcal{C}}},p)\subseteq\map_{\mathrm{coCart}({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}})_{\totalCategory({\underline{I}})}}(\pi_{{\mathcal{C}}},p)
consists precisely of those components of functors over
\totalCategory({\underline{I}})
(in the left diagram)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\totalCategory(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\times_{{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}}\totalCategory({\underline{I}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{E}_{F}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces=}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{I},\mathcal{E}_{F})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\totalCategory({\underline{I}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{I},\underline{I})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{{\mathcal{C}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{{\mathcal{C}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}

preserving cocartesian morphisms over
\totalCategory(\underline{I})
. Since the cocartesian morphisms in the cocartesian fibration
\pi_{{\mathcal{C}}}:\totalCategory(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\times_{{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}}\totalCategory({\underline{I}})\rightarrow\totalCategory(\underline{I})
are precisely the morphisms of
\totalCategory(\underline{I})
and an equivalence in
{\mathcal{C}}
, we see that this condition corresponds in the curried version on the right to those functors landing in
\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\underline{I}\mathrm{-cocart}}(\underline{I},\mathcal{E}_{F})
. Finally for the statement about the case of factoring over
\underline{\mathcal{S}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
recall that unstraightening brings us to left fibrations
\mathcal{E}_{F}\rightarrow\totalCategory(\underline{I})
, and since in left fibrations all morphisms are cocartesian, we need not have imposed the condition above. This shows us that we have a bijection of components

\pi_{0}\map_{\mathrm{coCart}(\totalCategory(\underline{I}))}(\pi_{{\mathcal{C}}},p)\simeq\pi_{0}\map_{\mathrm{coCart}({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}})}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{\Gamma}_{T}^{\underline{I}\mathrm{-cocart}}(p))

We now need to show that this would already imply that we have an equivalence of mapping
spaces
. For this, we will need to first construct a map of spaces realising the bijection above. First note that we have a map of cocartesian fibrations over
\totalCategory(\underline{I})

\varepsilon:\underline{\Gamma}^{\underline{I}\mathrm{-cocart}}_{T}(p)\times\underline{I}\longrightarrow\mathcal{E}_{F}

from the evaluation. Therefore we get the following maps of spaces

\begin{split}&\map_{\mathrm{coCart}({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}})}(-,\underline{\Gamma}^{\underline{I}\mathrm{-cocart}}_{T}(p))\\
&\xrightarrow{\underline{I}\times-}\map_{\mathrm{coCart}(\totalCategory(\underline{I}))}(\underline{I}\times-,\underline{I}\times\underline{\Gamma}^{\underline{I}\mathrm{-cocart}}_{T}(p))\\
&\xrightarrow{\varepsilon_{*}}\map_{\mathrm{coCart}(\totalCategory(\underline{I}))}(\underline{I}\times-,\mathcal{E}_{F})\end{split}

(1)

On the other hand, we know by the pullback definition of
\underline{\Gamma}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
that

\map_{\mathrm{coCart}({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}})}(-,\underline{\Gamma}_{T}(p))\simeq\map_{\mathrm{coCart}({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}})_{/\totalCategory(\underline{I})}}(\underline{I}\times-,\mathcal{E}_{F})

(2)

and so the comparison map
Eq.

1
is induced by this equivalence. Our bijection on components then gives that the equivalence
Eq.

2
restricts to an equivalence of spaces
Eq.

1
. This completes the proof of the result.
∎

As far as we are aware the following proof strategy first appeared in
[
GHN17
,
\lx@sectionsign 5
]
.

G)\big)\simeq\underline{\nattrans}_{{\mathcal{T}}}\big(y_{\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}},F^{*}\circ y_{\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}}\circ G)\big)

But then now we have the sequence of equivalences

\begin{split}\underline{\nattrans}_{{\mathcal{T}}}\big(y_{\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}},F^{*}\circ y_{\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}}\circ G)\big)&\simeq\underline{\nattrans}_{{\mathcal{T}}}\big(F_{!}\circ y_{\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}},y_{\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}}\circ G)\big)\\
&\simeq\underline{\nattrans}_{{\mathcal{T}}}\big(y_{\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}}\circ F,y_{\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}}\circ G)\big)\\
&\simeq\underline{\nattrans}_{T}(F,G)\end{split}

where the last equivalence is by
3.3.3
and the second by the square
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y_{\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y_{\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F_{!}}

which commutes by functoriality of presheaves.
∎

Definition 3.4.4
.

A
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor is called
{\mathcal{T}}
-faithful if it is so fibrewise, where an ordinary functor is called faithful if it induces component inclusions on mapping spaces.

Observation 3.4.5
.

For
f:X\rightarrow Y
a map of spaces, it being an inclusion of components is equivalent to the condition that for each
x\in X
, the fibre
\fib_{f(x)}\big(X\rightarrow Y\big)
is contractible. On the other hand, it is an equivalence if and only if for each
y\in Y
, the fibre
\fib_{y}\big(f:X\rightarrow Y\big)
is contractible. We learnt of this formulation and of the following proof in the unparametrised case from
[
Lei22
, Appendix B]
.

Corollary 3.4.6
.

Let
F:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
be a
{\mathcal{T}}
–(fully) faithful functor and
\underline{I}
another
{\mathcal{T}}
–category. Then
F_{*}:\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\rightarrow\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
is again
{\mathcal{T}}
–(fully) faithful.

Proof.

Since
{\mathcal{T}}
–(fully) faithfulness was defined as a fibrewise condition, we just assume without loss of generality that
{\mathcal{T}}
has a final object and work on global sections. In the faithful case, let
\varphi,\psi:\underline{I}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
be two
{\mathcal{T}}
–functors. We need to show that

\underline{\nattrans}_{\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})}(\varphi,\psi)\longrightarrow\underline{\nattrans}_{\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})}(F\varphi,F\psi)

is an inclusion of components. By the preceeding observation, we need to show that for each
\eta\in\nattrans_{\func_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})}(\varphi,\psi)
, the fibre

\underline{\fib}_{\eta}\big(\underline{\nattrans}_{\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})}(\varphi,\psi)\rightarrow\underline{\nattrans}_{\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})}(F\varphi,F\psi)\big)\in\Gamma(\underline{\mathcal{S}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}})

is contractible. But then we are now in position to use
3.4.3
:

\begin{split}&\underline{\fib}_{\eta}\Big(\underline{\nattrans}_{\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})}(\varphi,\psi)\rightarrow\underline{\nattrans}_{\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{I},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})}(F\varphi,F\psi)\Big)\\
&\simeq\underline{\lim}_{(x\rightarrow y)\in\underline{\twistedArrow}_{T}(\underline{I})}\underline{\fib}_{\eta}\Big(\mathchoice{\mbox{\uline{\phantom{$\displaystyle\map$}}\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\color[rgb]{1,1,1}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip 0.0pt\raisebox{0.5pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip 0.19133pt\raisebox{0.46193pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip 0.35355pt\raisebox{0.35355pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip 0.46193pt\raisebox{0.19133pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip 0.5pt\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip 0.46193pt\raisebox{-0.19133pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip &\simeq\underline{\lim}_{(x\rightarrow y)\in\underline{\twistedArrow}_{T}(\underline{I})}\ast_{{\mathcal{T}}}\simeq\ast_{T}\end{split}

as was to be shown, where the second last step is by our hypothesis that

–faithful. The case of
