∎

3.5
Recollections: filtered colimits and Ind-completions

Construction 3.5.1
.

Let
\kappa
be a regular cardinal. We define the
{\mathcal{T}}
-Ind-completion
functor
\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}\colon\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}\rightarrow\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
to be the one obtained by applying
\func({\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}},-)
to the ordinary functor
\mathrm{Ind}_{\kappa}\colon\mathrm{Cat}\rightarrow\mathrm{Cat}
.

Notation 3.5.2
.

We will write
\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\mathrm{filt}}
for the full
{\mathcal{T}}
–subcategory of parametrised functors preserving fibrewise
\omega
–filtered colimits, and similarly
\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\kappa\operatorname{-filt}}
for those that preserve fibrewise
\kappa
-filtered colimits.

Remark 3.5.3
.

This agrees with the definition given in the recent paper
[
Sha22
]
by virtue of the paragraph after Theorem D therein. As indicated there,
\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
is the minimal
{\mathcal{T}}
–subcategory of
\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
generated by
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
under fibrewise
\kappa
-filtered colimits. In more detail,
[
Sha22
, Rmk. 9.4]
showed that the fibrewise presheaf construction
\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\text{fb}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
is a
{\mathcal{T}}
–full subcategory of the
{\mathcal{T}}
–presheaf
\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
via the fibrewise left Kan extension. In particular, this means that
\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\text{fb}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\subseteq\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
preserves fibrewise colimits. On the other hand, by construction and
[
Lur09
, Cor. 5.3.5.4]
,
\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\subseteq\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\text{fb}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
is the minimal
{\mathcal{T}}
–subcategory generated by
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
under fibrewise
\kappa
-filtered colimits. Therefore, in total, we see that
\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\subseteq\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
is the
{\mathcal{T}}
–subcategory generated by
{\mathcal{C}}
under fibrewise
\kappa
-filtered colimits.

Proposition 3.5.4

(Universal property of
\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}
, “
[
Lur09
, Prop. 5.3.5.10]
”)
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
be
{\mathcal{T}}
–categories where
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is small and
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
has fibrewise small
\kappa
-filtered colimits. Then:

(1)

\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\subseteq\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
is the
{\mathcal{T}}
–subcategory generated by
{\mathcal{C}}
under fibrewise
\kappa
-filtered colimits.

(2)

The
{\mathcal{T}}
–inclusion
i:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\hookrightarrow\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
induces an equivalence

i^{*}:\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\kappa\operatorname{-filt}}(\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}),\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})\longrightarrow\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})

Proof.

Part (1) is by the remark above. For part (2), we show that the
{\mathcal{T}}
–left Kan extension functor
i_{!}:\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})\longrightarrow\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\kappa\operatorname{-filt}}(\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}),\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
exists and is an inverse to
i^{*}
. To do this, it will be enough to show that functors
F:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
can be
{\mathcal{T}}
–left Kan extended to
i_{!}F:\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
and that functors
F:\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
which preserves fibrewise
\kappa
-filtered colimits satisfy that
i_{!}i^{*}F\Rightarrow F
is an equivalence. This will be enough since we would have shown the natural equivalence
i_{!}i^{*}\simeq\mathrm{id}
, and
3.1.14
gives that
i^{*}i_{!}\simeq\mathrm{id}
always.

To show that the
{\mathcal{T}}
–left Kan extension exists, consider the diagram
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

where
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\subseteq\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}^{\prime}
is a strongly
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimit preserving inclusion into a
{\mathcal{T}}
–cocomplete
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}^{\prime}
using the opposite
{\mathcal{T}}
–Yoneda embedding. In particular by hypothesis
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
is closed under
\kappa
-filtered colimits in
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}^{\prime}
. The bottom dashed map is gotten from
3.3.7
, and so strongly preserves
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits. Hence restriction to
\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
lands in
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
so we get middle dashed map, and by the following
3.5.5
, this is a left Kan extension.

Now we show that if
F
preserves fibrewise
\kappa
-filtered colimits, then the canonical comparison
i_{!}i^{*}F\Rightarrow F
is an equivalence. Again, by
3.1.14
we know that both sides agree on
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\subseteq\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
. Also, both sides preserve
\kappa
-filtered colimits by assumption. Hence, by statement (1) of the proposition, we see that it must be an equivalence as was to be shown.
∎

Lemma 3.5.5
.

Suppose we have fully faithful functors
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\xhookrightarrow{i}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\xhookrightarrow{j}\underline{\mathcal{E}}
and functors
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\xrightarrow{f}\underline{\mathcal{A}}\xhookrightarrow{y}\underline{\mathcal{B}}
, where
\underline{B}
is
{\mathcal{T}}
–(co)complete. Suppose we have a factorisation
j^{*}j_{!}i_{!}(y\circ f)\colon\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\xrightarrow{\overline{f}}\underline{\mathcal{A}}\xhookrightarrow{y}\underline{\mathcal{B}}
. Then
\overline{f}\simeq i_{!}f\colon\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathcal{A}}
.

Proof.

Let
\varphi\colon\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathcal{A}}
. We need to show that
\underline{\nattrans}(\overline{f},\varphi)\simeq\underline{\nattrans}(f,i^{*}\varphi)
. We compute:

\begin{split}\underline{\nattrans}(\overline{f},\varphi)&\simeq\underline{\nattrans}(y\circ\overline{f},y\circ\varphi)\\
&=\underline{\nattrans}(j^{*}j_{!}i_{!}(y\circ f),y\circ\varphi)\\
&\simeq\underline{\nattrans}(y\circ f,i^{*}j^{*}j_{*}(y\circ\varphi))\\
&\simeq\underline{\nattrans}(y\circ f,i^{*}(y\circ\varphi)\simeq\underline{\nattrans}(f,i^{*}\varphi)\end{split}

where the first and last equivalences are since
y
was fully faithful; the fourth equivalence is since
j
was fully faithful and so
3.1.14
applies. The relevant Kan extensions exist since
\underline{\mathcal{B}}
was assumed to be
{\mathcal{T}}
–(co)complete.
∎

We learnt of the following proof method from Markus Land.

Lemma 3.5.6
.

For
{\mathcal{C}},{\mathcal{D}}\in\mathrm{Cat}
, we have a functor

\func({\mathcal{C}},{\mathcal{D}})\rightarrow\func(\mathrm{Ind}({\mathcal{C}}),\mathrm{Ind}({\mathcal{D}}))
that takes
F:{\mathcal{C}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{D}}
to
\mathrm{Ind}(F):\mathrm{Ind}({\mathcal{C}})\rightarrow\mathrm{Ind}({\mathcal{D}})
.

Proof.

We know that
\mathrm{Ind}(\mathcal{E}\times{\mathcal{C}})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(\mathcal{E})\times\mathrm{Ind}({\mathcal{C}})
.
In particular, we get functors

\Delta^{n}\times\mathrm{Ind}({\mathcal{C}})\longrightarrow\mathrm{Ind}(\Delta^{n}\times{\mathcal{C}})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}(\Delta^{n})\times\mathrm{Ind}({\mathcal{C}})

natural in both
\Delta^{n}
and
{\mathcal{C}}
. These then induce a map of simplicial spaces

\func(\Delta^{\bullet}\times{\mathcal{C}},{\mathcal{D}})^{\simeq}\longrightarrow\func(\mathrm{Ind}(\Delta^{\bullet}\times{\mathcal{C}}),\mathrm{Ind}({\mathcal{D}}))^{\simeq}\longrightarrow\func(\Delta^{\bullet}\times\mathrm{Ind}({\mathcal{C}}),\mathrm{Ind}({\mathcal{D}}))^{\simeq}

where the first map is just by the
(\infty,1)
–functoriality of
\mathrm{Ind}
. Via the complete Segal space model of
\infty
-categories, we see that we have the desired functor which behaves as in the statement by looking at the case
\bullet=0
.
∎

Lemma 3.5.7

(Ind adjunctions)
.

Let
f:{\mathcal{C}}\rightleftarrows{\mathcal{D}}:g
be an adjunction. Then we also have an adjunction

F\coloneqq\mathrm{Ind}(f):\mathrm{Ind}({\mathcal{C}})\rightleftarrows\mathrm{Ind}({\mathcal{D}}):\mathrm{Ind}(g)=:G
.

Proof.

By
[
RV19
, Def. 1.1.2]
we know that such an adjunction is tantamount to the data of
\eta:\mathrm{id}_{{\mathcal{C}}}\Rightarrow gf
and
\varepsilon:fg\Rightarrow\mathrm{id}_{{\mathcal{D}}}
such that we have the triangle identities
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces=}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{D}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{D}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{D}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varepsilon}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\eta}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}^{\Rightarrow}_{\mathrm{id}_{g}}}

and the analogous other triangle. Now, we have

\func({\mathcal{C}},{\mathcal{C}})\rightarrow\func(\mathrm{Ind}({\mathcal{C}}),\mathrm{Ind}({\mathcal{C}}))
by
3.5.6
and so the the triangle identity on the source gets sent to a triangle identity on the target.
∎

Theorem 3.5.8

(Diagram decomposition,
[
Sha22
, Thm. 8.1]
)
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
be a
{\mathcal{T}}
–category,
J
a category, and
p_{\bullet}:J\rightarrow({\mathrm{Cat}}_{{\mathcal{T}}})_{/\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}}
a functor with colimit the
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor
p:\underline{K}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
and suppose that for all
j\in J
, the
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor
p_{j}:\underline{K}_{j}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
admits a
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimit
\sigma_{j}
. Then the
\sigma_{j}
’s assemble to a
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor
\sigma_{\bullet}:\tconstant_{\mathcal{T}}(J)\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
so that if
\sigma_{\bullet}
admits a
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimit
\sigma
, then
p
admits a
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimit given by
\sigma
.

Corollary 3.5.9

(Parametrised filtered colimit decomposition, “
[
Lur09
, Cor. 4.2.3.11]
”)
.

Let
\tau\ll\kappa
be regular cardinals and
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
be a
{\mathcal{T}}
–category admitting
\tau
-small
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits and fibrewise colimits indexed by
\kappa
-small
\tau
-filtered posets. Then for any
\kappa
-small
{\mathcal{T}}
–diagram
d:\underline{K}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
, its
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimit in
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
exists and can be decomposed as a fibrewise
\kappa
-small
\tau
-filtered colimit whose vertices are
\tau
-small
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits of
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
.

Proof.

Let
J
denote the poset of
\tau
-small
{\mathcal{T}}
–subcategories of
\underline{K}
. It is clearly
\tau
-filtered and moreover it is
\kappa
-small by the hypothesis that
\tau\ll\kappa
. We can therefore apply the theorem above since the associated
\sigma_{\bullet}:\tconstant_{\mathcal{T}}(J)\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
will admit a
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimit by hypothesis.
∎

4
Preliminaries: atomic orbital base categories

will be assumed to be both orbital
and

Definition 4.1.2
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
strongly admit finite
{\mathcal{T}}
–coproducts and
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
strongly admit finite
{\mathcal{T}}
–products. Then we say that a
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor
F:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
is
{\mathcal{T}}
-semiadditive
if it sends finite
{\mathcal{T}}
–coproducts to finite
{\mathcal{T}}
–products. We say that a
{\mathcal{T}}
–category
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
strongly admitting finite
{\mathcal{T}}
–products and
{\mathcal{T}}
–coproducts is
{\mathcal{T}}
–semiadditive
if the identity functor is
{\mathcal{T}}
–semiadditive. If moreover
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
has fibrewise pushouts and
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
has fibrewise pullbacks, then we say that
F
is
{\mathcal{T}}
–linear
if it is
{\mathcal{T}}
–semiadditive and sends fibrewise pushouts to fibrewise pullbacks. We write
\underline{\func}^{\underline{\mathrm{sadd}}}_{T}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
(resp.
\underline{\mathrm{Lin}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
) for the
{\mathcal{T}}
–full subcategories of
\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
consisting of the
{\mathcal{T}}
–semiadditive functors (resp.
{\mathcal{T}}
–linear functors).

Proposition 4.1.4

(
{\mathcal{T}}
–semiadditivisation,
[
Nar16
, Prop. 5.11]
)
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
be a
{\mathcal{T}}
–category strongly admitting finite
{\mathcal{T}}
–products. Then the functor
\underline{\cmonoid}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
induced by the inclusion
\underline{\ast}\hookrightarrow\underline{\mathrm{Fin}}_{*{\mathcal{T}}}
from
4.1.1
(4) is an equivalence if and only if
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
were
{\mathcal{T}}
–semiadditive.

Notation 4.1.6
.

We write
\func_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{{\mathrm{ex}}},\func_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{{\mathrm{lex}}},
and
\func_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{{\mathrm{rex}}}
for the category of
{\mathcal{T}}
–functors which strongly preserve finite
{\mathcal{T}}
–(co)limits, strongly preserve finite
{\mathcal{T}}
–limits, and strongly preserve finite
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits, respectively.

.

4.2
Parametrised symmetric monoidality and commutative algebras

Recollections 4.2.1
.

There is a notion of
{\mathcal{T}}
–operads mimicking the notion of
\infty
-operads, in the sense of
[
Lur17
,
\lx@sectionsign 2.1
]
, due to Nardin in
[
Nar17
,
\lx@sectionsign 3
]
and further developed in
[
NS22
, §2]
. A
{\mathcal{T}}
–symmetric monoidal category is then a
{\mathcal{T}}
–category
{\mathcal{C}}^{\underline{\otimes}}
equipped with a cocartesian fibration over
\underline{\mathrm{Fin}}_{*{\mathcal{T}}}
satisfying the
{\mathcal{T}}
–operad axioms analogous to the operad axioms of
[
Lur17
, Definition 2.1.1.10]
. Alternatively, the
{\mathcal{T}}
–category of
{\mathcal{T}}
–symmetric monoidal categories is also given as
\underline{\cmonoid}(\underline{\mathrm{Cat}})
much like in the unparametrised setting. Furthermore, there is also the attendant notion of
{\mathcal{T}}
-inert morphisms
defined as those morphisms in
\underline{\mathrm{Fin}}_{*{\mathcal{T}}}
where the the map
W\rightarrow U^{\prime}
is an equivalence (cf. the span notation in
Eq.

3
). The
{\mathcal{T}}
–category of
{\mathcal{T}}
-commutative algebras

–full subcategory of functors over
\underline{\mathrm{Fin}}_{*{\mathcal{T}}}
preserving
{\mathcal{T}}
–inert morphisms. We refer the reader to the original source
[
Nar17
,
\lx@sectionsign 3.1
]
or to
[
NS22
, §2]
for details on this.

Terminology 4.2.2
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\otimes}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}^{\underline{\otimes}}
be
{\mathcal{T}}
–symmetric monoidal categories. By a
{\mathcal{T}}
-symmetric monoidal localisation

L^{\underline{\otimes}}:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\otimes}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}^{\underline{\otimes}}
we mean a
{\mathcal{T}}
–symmetric monoidal functor whose underlying
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor is a
{\mathcal{T}}
–Bousfield localisation. By the proof of
[
Nar17
, Prop. 3.5]
, we see that the
{\mathcal{T}}
–right adjoint canonically refines to a
{\mathcal{T}}
–lax symmetric functor. Hence in this situation we obtain a relative adjunction over
\underline{\mathrm{Fin}}_{*{\mathcal{T}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\otimes}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}^{\underline{\otimes}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\underline{\mathrm{Fin}}_{*{\mathcal{T}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L^{\underline{\otimes}}}

in the sense of
[
Lur17
,
\lx@sectionsign 7.3.2
]
whose counit is moreover an equivalence.

comes with a canonical

–commutative algebra map
\eta^{\prime}:A\rightarrow R^{\prime}L^{\prime}A

A

L\dashv R
unit

{\mathcal{T}}
–commutative algebras, then by universality of
\eta^{\prime}

4.3
Indexed (co)products of categories

We now investigate various permanence properties of indexed products on categories. To begin with, recall the following for which a good summary is
[
QS22
, Ex. 5.20]
.

Construction 4.3.1

(Indexed products of categories)
.

Let
f:U\rightarrow U^{\prime}
be a map of finite
{\mathcal{T}}
–sets. Then
2.1.16
gives us the equivalences in

f^{*}:\func(\totalCategory(\underline{U}^{\prime}),\mathrm{Cat})\simeq\func_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{U}^{\prime},\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}_{{\mathcal{T}}})\rightarrow\func_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{U},\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}_{{\mathcal{T}}})\simeq\func(\totalCategory(\underline{U}),\mathrm{Cat})

This has a right adjoint
f_{*}
(also written
\prod_{f}
). Thus, for
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\in\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}_{\underline{U}}
and
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\in\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}_{\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}}
we have

\underline{\func}_{\underline{U}^{\prime}}\Big(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}},f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\Big)\simeq\underline{\func}_{\underline{U}}(f^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})

By setting
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}=\underline{V}
we see that
f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is a
{\mathcal{T}}_{/U^{\prime}}
–category with
V
–fibre given by

\func_{\underline{U}}(\underline{U}_{\underline{V}},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\simeq\prod_{O\in\operatorname{Orbit}(U\times_{U^{\prime}}V)}{\mathcal{C}}_{O}

where
\underline{U}_{\underline{V}}
is the model for the corepresentable
{\mathcal{T}}
–category associated to
U\times_{U^{\prime}}V
whose fibre over
[W\rightarrow U]
is given by the space of commutative squares in
\mathrm{Fin}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U^{\prime}}

Lemma 4.3.2

(Indexed constructions preserve adjunctions)
.

Let
f:W\rightarrow V
be in
{\mathcal{T}}
. Let
L:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightleftarrows\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}:R
be a
{\mathcal{T}}_{/W}
–adjunction and
M:\underline{\mathcal{A}}\rightleftarrows\underline{\mathcal{B}}:N
be a
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
–adjunction. Then

f_{*}L:f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightleftarrows f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}:f_{*}R\quad\quad\quad f^{*}M:f^{*}\underline{\mathcal{A}}\rightleftarrows f^{*}\underline{\mathcal{B}}:f^{*}N

are
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
– and
{\mathcal{T}}_{/W}
–adjunctions respectively.

Proof.

By
2.2.7
, we need to show that these induce fibrewise adjunctions. This is clear for the pair
(f^{*}M,f^{*}N)
since fibrewise they are the same as
(M,N)
; for
(f_{*}L,f_{*}R)
, we use that (unparametrised) products of adjunctions are again adjunctions.
∎

Lemma 4.3.3

((Co)unit of indexed products)
.

The
{\mathcal{T}}
–cofree category
\underline{\mathrm{Cat}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
strongly admits
{\mathcal{T}}
–products, and for
f:W\rightarrow V
,
X\in{\mathcal{T}}_{/W}
, and
Y\in{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
, we have that

(f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})_{Y}\simeq\prod_{M\in\operatorname{Orbit}(Y\times_{V}W)}{\mathcal{D}}_{M}
and moreover:

•

The unit is given by

\eta=F^{*}:{\mathcal{C}}_{Y}\longrightarrow(f_{*}f^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})_{Y}=\prod_{M\in\operatorname{Orbit}(Y\times_{V}W)}{\mathcal{C}}_{M}
where
F:Y\times_{V}W\rightarrow Y
is the structure map from the pullback,

•

The counit is given by

\varepsilon=\mathrm{proj}:(f^{*}f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})_{X}=\prod_{N\in\operatorname{Orbit}(X\times_{V}W)}{\mathcal{D}}_{N}\longrightarrow{\mathcal{D}}_{X}
the component projection (see the proof for why we have this).

Proof.

We know that
f^{*}:\func(({\mathcal{T}}_{/V})^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Cat})\longrightarrow\func(({\mathcal{T}}_{/W})^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Cat})
abstractly has a right adjoint
f_{*}
via right Kan extension, and the formula for ordinary right Kan extensions gives us the required description (which is also gotten from
4.3.1
).

To describe the (co)units, we have to check the triangle identities

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}f_{*}f^{*}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{*}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{*}f^{*}f_{*}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}\eta}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varepsilon_{f^{*}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\eta_{f_{*}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{*}\varepsilon}

(4)

First of all we clarify why we have the counit map as stated. For this it will be helpful to write carefully the datum
\varphi:X\rightarrow W
instead of just
X
. Consider
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X\times_{V}W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi}

\lrcorner

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f\varphi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

This shows that
X
is a retract of
X\times_{V}W
, and so by atomicity, we get that
X
was an orbit in the orbit decomposition of
X\times_{V}W
, and so the component projection
\varepsilon:(f^{*}f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})_{X}=\prod_{N\in\operatorname{Orbit}(X\times_{V}W)}{\mathcal{D}}_{N}\longrightarrow{\mathcal{D}}_{X}
is well-defined

To check the first triangle identity, let
(\varphi:X\rightarrow W)\in{\mathcal{T}}_{/W}
and consider
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod_{a}N_{a}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod_{a}\xi_{a}}

\lrcorner

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f\varphi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

where one of the
N_{a}
’s is
X
, by the argument above. Then we have that the composition in the first triangle in
Eq.

4
is

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Big((f^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})_{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(f^{*}f_{*}f^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})_{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(f^{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})_{X}\Big)\>\simeq\>\Big({\mathcal{C}}_{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\prod_{a}{\mathcal{C}}_{N_{a}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}}_{X}\Big)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}\eta}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varepsilon_{f^{*}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\prod_{a}\xi_{a}^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{proj}}

which is of course the identity since
\xi_{a}=\mathrm{id}
in the case

.

The second triangle identity is slightly more intricate. Let
(\psi:Y\rightarrow V)\in{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
. We consider two pullbacks (where the right square is for each
b
appearing in the left square)
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod_{b}M_{b}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod_{c_{b}}\widetilde{M}_{c_{b}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M_{b}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod_{b}\zeta_{b}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod_{b}\rho_{b}}

\lrcorner

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod_{c_{b}}\ell_{c_{b}}}

\lrcorner

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f\rho_{b}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

From this, the composition in the second triangle in

is

\begin{split}&\Big((f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})_{Y}\xlongrightarrow{\eta_{f_{*}}}(f_{*}f^{*}f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})_{Y}\xlongrightarrow{f_{*}\varepsilon}(f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})_{Y}\Big)\\
&\simeq\Big(\prod_{b}{\mathcal{D}}_{M_{b}}\xlongrightarrow{\prod_{b}\prod_{c_{b}}\ell^{*}_{c_{b}}}\prod_{b}\prod_{c_{b}}{\mathcal{D}}_{\widetilde{M}_{c_{b}}}\xrightarrow{\prod_{b}\mathrm{proj}}\prod_{b}{\mathcal{D}}_{M_{b}}\Big)\end{split}

which is the identity map as wanted since

is one of the orbits in

by the argument above. Here we have used the diagram
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})_{Y}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\prod_{b}(f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})_{M_{b}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\prod_{b}{\mathcal{D}}_{M_{b}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\prod_{b}\prod_{c_{b}}{\mathcal{D}}_{\widetilde{M}_{c_{b}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\eta_{f_{*}}=\prod_{b}\zeta_{b}^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\prod_{b}\prod_{c_{b}}\ell^{*}_{c_{b}}}

to analyse the map

, which in turn comes from the top square in
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod_{c_{b}}\widetilde{M}_{c_{b}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M_{b}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod_{b}M_{b}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V}

\lrcorner

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod_{c_{b}}\ell_{c_{b}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\coprod_{c_{b}}\ell_{c_{b}}}

\lrcorner

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\zeta_{b}}

\lrcorner

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

4.4

We now recall the notion of

,
\lx@sectionsign 3.3

[

,
\lx@sectionsign 5.1
]
.

Definition 4.4.1
.

Let

be a map in
\mathrm{Fin}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
,

,

–functor. Then we say that

–distributive

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U^{\prime}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V^{\prime}}

and

–colimit diagram

, the

Construction 4.4.2

(Norms of categories)
.

Let
f:U\rightarrow V
be a map in
\mathrm{Fin}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
and
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
a
{\mathcal{T}}_{/U}
–category which is
{\mathcal{T}}_{/U}
–cocomplete. Then we define the
f
-norm

f_{\otimes}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
, if it exists, to be a
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
–cocomplete category admitting a
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
–distributive functor
\tau:f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow f_{\otimes}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
such that for any other
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
–cocomplete category, the following functor is an equivalence

\tau^{*}:{\func}^{L}_{\underline{V}}(f_{\otimes}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})\rightarrow{\func}^{\delta}_{\underline{V}}(f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})

We also write this as
f_{\otimes}=\bigotimes_{f}
.

Lemma 4.4.3

(Norms preserve adjunctions)
.

Let
F:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightleftarrows\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}:G
be a
{\mathcal{T}}_{/U}
–adjunction such that
G
itself admits a right adjoint and
f:U\rightarrow V
be a map in
\mathrm{Fin}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
. Then this induces a
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
–adjunction

f_{\otimes}F:f_{\otimes}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightleftarrows f_{\otimes}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}:f_{\otimes}G

Proof.

Recall from
4.3.2
that we have a
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
–adjunction

f_{*}F:f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightleftarrows f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}:f_{*}G
and since
G
itself has a right adjoint, both
f_{*}F
and
f_{*}G
strongly preserve
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
–colimits. Now observe that this adjunction can equivalently be encoded by the data of morphisms

\big(\eta\colon\mathrm{id}\Rightarrow(f_{*}G)\circ(f_{*}F)\big)\in\underline{\func}^{L}_{\underline{V}}(f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})

\big(\varepsilon\colon(f_{*}F)\circ(f_{*}G)\Rightarrow\mathrm{id}\big)\in\underline{\func}^{L}_{\underline{V}}(f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}},f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})

whose images under the functors

(f_{*}F)_{*}\colon{\func}^{L}_{\underline{V}}(f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})\rightarrow{\func}^{L}_{\underline{V}}(f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})

(f_{*}F)^{*}\colon{\func}^{L}_{\underline{V}}(f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}},f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})\rightarrow{\func}^{L}_{\underline{V}}(f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})

respectively compose to a morphism equivalent to the identity
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{*}F}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(f_{*}F)\circ(f_{*}G)\circ(f_{*}F)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{*}F}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{*}F(\eta)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varepsilon_{f_{*}F}}

and similarly for the other triangle identity. Now, we have commutative squares
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{\otimes}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{\otimes}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{*}F}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{*}G}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{\otimes}F}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{\otimes}G}

where
\varphi:f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow f_{\otimes}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
,
\psi:f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\rightarrow f_{\otimes}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
are the universal distributive functors: this is since
G
strongly preserves
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits by hypothesis. This yields
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\func}^{L}_{\underline{V}}(f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\func}^{L}_{\underline{V}}(f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\func}^{L}_{\underline{V}}(f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}},f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\func}^{\delta}_{\underline{V}}(f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},f_{\otimes}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\func}^{\delta}_{\underline{V}}(f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},f_{\otimes}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\func}^{\delta}_{\underline{V}}(f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}},f_{\otimes}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\func}^{L}_{\underline{V}}(f_{\otimes}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},f_{\otimes}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\func}^{L}_{\underline{V}}(f_{\otimes}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},f_{\otimes}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\func}^{L}_{\underline{V}}(f_{\otimes}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}},f_{\otimes}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi_{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(f_{*}F)_{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi_{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(f_{*}F)^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi_{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(f_{\otimes}F)_{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(f_{\otimes}F)^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(f_{\otimes}F)_{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(f_{\otimes}F)^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}

Then the morphism
\big(\eta:\mathrm{id}\Rightarrow(f_{*}G)\circ(f_{*}F)\big)\in\underline{\func}^{L}_{\underline{V}}(f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},f_{*}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
in the top left corner gets sent to a morphism
\big(\widetilde{\eta}:\mathrm{id}\Rightarrow(f_{\otimes}G)\circ(f_{\otimes}F)\big)\in\underline{\func}^{L}_{\underline{V}}(f_{\otimes}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}},f_{\otimes}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
in the bottom left, and similarly for
\varepsilon
. Then by the characterisation of adjunctions above, since the composition of the images in the middle top term is equivalent to the identity, so is the image in the middle bottom term, that is, we have the commuting diagram
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{\otimes}F}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(f_{\otimes}F)\circ(f_{\otimes}G)\circ(f_{\otimes}F)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{\otimes}F}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{\otimes}F(\widetilde{\eta})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widetilde{\varepsilon}_{f_{\otimes}F}}

and similarly for the other triangle identity. This witnesses that we have a
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
–adjunction
f_{\otimes}F\dashv f_{\otimes}G
as required.
∎

Remark 4.4.4
.

Let
V,W\in{\mathcal{T}}
and
{\mathcal{C}}^{\underline{\otimes}}
a
{\mathcal{T}}
–symmetric monoidal category. Concretely speaking, we get the structure of tensor products and norm functors as follows:

•

(Tensor functor): Consider the morphism in
\underline{\mathrm{Fin}}_{*{\mathcal{T}}}
given by
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V\coprod V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V\coprod V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nabla}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nabla}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nabla}

The cocartesian lifts along this morphism give us the tensor product

\otimes:{\mathcal{C}}_{V}\times{\mathcal{C}}_{V}\simeq{\mathcal{C}}_{V\coprod V}\longrightarrow{\mathcal{C}}_{V}

•

(Norm functor): Suppose
f:V\rightarrow W
is a morphism in
{\mathcal{T}}
. Consider
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

The cocartesian lifts along this morphism give us the norm functor

\mathrm{N}^{f}:{\mathcal{C}}_{V}\simeq{\mathcal{C}}^{\underline{\otimes}}_{[f:V\rightarrow W]}\longrightarrow{\mathcal{C}}^{\underline{\otimes}}_{[W=W]}\simeq{\mathcal{C}}_{W}

Note that it might have been tempting to define the norm functor as the pushforward along the more obvious morphism
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces V}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

instead, but the problem is that this is not a morphism in
\underline{\mathrm{Fin}}_{*{\mathcal{T}}}
because by definition the bottom right map needs to be the identity!

5
Parametrised smallness adjectives

We now introduce the notion of
{\mathcal{T}}
–compactness and
{\mathcal{T}}
–idempotent-completeness. Not only are these notions crucial in proving the characterisations of
{\mathcal{T}}
–presentables in
6.1.2
, they are also fundamental for the applications we have in mind for parametrised algebraic K–theory in
[
Hil22a
]
. The moral of this section is that these are essentially fibrewise notions and should present no conceptual difficulties to those already familiar with the unparametrised versions. Recall that we will assume throughout that
{\mathcal{T}}
is orbital.

5.1
Parametrised compactness

Recall that an object
X
in a category
{\mathcal{C}}
is compact if
\map_{{\mathcal{C}}}(X,-):{\mathcal{C}}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}
commutes with filtered colimits (cf.
[
Lur09
,
\lx@sectionsign 5.3.4
]
). In this subsection we introduce the parametrised analogue of this notion and study its interaction with Ind-completions.

Definition 5.1.1
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
be a
{\mathcal{T}}
–category and
V\in{\mathcal{T}}
. A
V
-object in
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
(ie. an object in
\func_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{V},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
) is
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
–
\kappa
-
compact
if it is fibrewise
\kappa
-compact. We will also use the terminology
parametrised-
\kappa
-compact objects
when we allow
V
to vary. We write
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\kappa}}
for the
{\mathcal{T}}
–subcategory of parametrised-
\kappa
-compact objects, that is,
(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\kappa}})_{V}
is given by the full subcategory of
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
–
\kappa
-compact objects.

Notation 5.1.2
.

We write
\underline{\func}_{{\mathcal{T}}}^{\underline{\kappa}}
for the full
{\mathcal{T}}
–subcategory of parametrised functors preserving parametrised
\kappa
-compact objects.

Warning 5.1.3
.

In general, for
V\in{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}
, the inclusion
(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\kappa}})_{V}\subseteq({\mathcal{C}}_{V})^{{\kappa}}
is not an equivalence - the point is that parametrised-
\kappa
-compactness must be preserved under the cocartesian lifts
f^{*}:{\mathcal{C}}_{V}\rightarrow{\mathcal{C}}_{W}
for all
f:W\rightarrow V
, but these do not preserve
\kappa
-compactness in general.

This definition of compactness makes sense by virtue of the following:

Proposition 5.1.4

(Characterisation of parametrised-compactness)
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
admit fibrewise
\kappa
-filtered
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits. A
{\mathcal{T}}
–object
C\in\func_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{\ast},\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
is
\kappa
–
{\mathcal{T}}
–compact in the sense above if and only if for all
V\in{\mathcal{T}}
and all fibrewise
\kappa
-filtered
{\mathcal{T}}_{/V}
–diagram

Observation 5.1.5
.

By the characterisation of
{\mathcal{T}}
–compactness above together with the
{\mathcal{T}}
–Yoneda
3.3.3
, and that
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits in
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor categories are computed in the target by
3.1.12
we see that the
{\mathcal{T}}
–Yoneda embedding lands in
\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})^{\underline{\kappa}}
.

Proposition 5.1.6

(
{\mathcal{T}}
–compact closure, “
[
Lur09
, Cor. 5.3.4.15]

5.2
Parametrised Ind-completions and accessibility

Proposition 5.2.1

(
\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}
fully faithfulness, “
[
Lur09
, Prop. 5.3.5.11]
”)
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
and
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\in\widehat{\mathrm{Cat}}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
which strongly admits fibrewise
\kappa
-filtered colimits. Suppose
F:\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
strongly preserves fibrewise
\kappa
-filtered colimits and
f=F\circ j:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
.

1.

If
f
is
{\mathcal{T}}
–fully faithful and the
{\mathcal{T}}
–essential image lands in
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}^{\underline{\kappa}}
, then
F
is
{\mathcal{T}}
–fully faithful.

2.

If
f
is
{\mathcal{T}}
–fully faithful, lands in
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}^{\underline{\kappa}}
, and the
{\mathcal{T}}
–essential image of
f
generates
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
under fibrewise
\kappa
-filtered colimits, then
F
is moreover a
{\mathcal{T}}
–equivalence.

Proposition 5.2.4

(“
[
Lur09
, Prop. 5.3.5.12]
”)
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathrm{Cat}_{{\mathcal{T}}}
and
\kappa
a regular cardinal. Then the canonical functor
F:\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}(\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})^{\underline{\kappa}})\rightarrow\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
is an equivalence.

Proof.

To see that
F
is an equivalence, we want to apply
5.2.1
. Let
j:\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})^{\underline{\kappa}}\hookrightarrow\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}(\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})^{\underline{\kappa}})
be the canonical embedding. That the composite
f\coloneqq F\circ j
is
{\mathcal{T}}
–fully faithful and lands in
\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})^{\underline{\kappa}}
is clear. To see that the essential image of
f
generates
\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
under fibrewise
\kappa
-filtered colimits, recall that any
X\in\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
can be written as a small
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimit of a diagram valued in
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\subseteq\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
by
3.3.6
. Then
3.5.9
gives
that
X
can be written as a fibrewise
\kappa
-filtered colimit taking values in
\underline{\mathcal{E}}\subseteq\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
where each object of
\underline{\mathcal{E}}
is itself a
\kappa
-small
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimit of some diagram taking values in
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\subseteq\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})^{\underline{\kappa}}.
But then by
5.1.6
we know that
\underline{\mathcal{E}}\subseteq\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})^{\underline{\kappa}}
, and so this completes the proof.
∎

Proposition 5.2.5

(Characterisation of
{\mathcal{T}}
–compacts in
{\mathcal{T}}
–presheaves, “
[
Lur09
, Prop. 5.3.4.17]

\kappa

5.1.4

0.19133pt\raisebox{-0.46193pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip 0.0pt\raisebox{-0.5pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip-0.19133pt\raisebox{-0.46193pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip-0.35355pt\raisebox{-0.35355pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip-0.46193pt\raisebox{-0.19133pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox to0.0pt{\hskip-0.5pt\raisebox{0.0pt}[0.0pt]{$\displaystyle\map$}\hss}\hbox Definition 5.2.6
.

Let
\kappa
be a regular cardinal and
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
a
{\mathcal{T}}
–category. We say that
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is
\kappa
–
{\mathcal{T}}
–
accessible
if there is a small
{\mathcal{T}}
–category
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{0}
and a
{\mathcal{T}}
–equivalence
\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{0})\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
. We say that
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is
{\mathcal{T}}
–
accessible
if it is
\kappa
–
{\mathcal{T}}
–accessible for some regular cardinal
\kappa
. A
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor out of a
{\mathcal{T}}
–accessible
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is said to be
{\mathcal{T}}
-accessible
if it strongly preserves all fibrewise
\kappa
-filtered colimits for some regular cardinal
\kappa
.

Lemma 5.2.7

(
{\mathcal{T}}
–accessibility of
{\mathcal{T}}
–adjoints, “
[
Lur09
, Prop. 5.4.7.7]
”)
.

Let
G:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\prime}
be a
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor between
{\mathcal{T}}
–accessibles. If
G
admits a right or a left
{\mathcal{T}}
–adjoint, then
G
is
{\mathcal{T}}
–accessible.

Proof.

The case of left
{\mathcal{T}}
–adjoints is clear since these strongly preserve all
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits, so suppose
G\dashv F
. Choose a regular cardinal
\kappa
so that
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\prime}
is
\kappa
-accessible, ie.
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\prime}=\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
for some
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
small. Consider the composite

\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\xrightarrow{j}\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\xrightarrow{F}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
. Since
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
is small there is a regular cardinal
\tau\gg\kappa
so that both
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is
\tau
-accessible and the essential image of
F\circ j
consists of
\tau
-
{\mathcal{T}}
–compact objects of
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
. We will show that
G
strongly preserves fibrewise
\tau
-filtered colimits.

Since
\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\subseteq\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
is stable under small
\tau
-filtered colimits by
3.5.4
it will suffice to prove that

G^{\prime}:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\xrightarrow{G}\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\rightarrow\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})

preserves fibrewise
\tau
-filtered colimits. Since colimits in presheaf categories are computed pointwise by
3.1.12
it suffices to show this when evaluated at each
D\in{\mathcal{D}}_{V}
for all
V\in{\mathcal{T}}
. Without loss of generality we just work with
D\in{\mathcal{D}}
, ie. a
{\mathcal{T}}
–object
D\in\func_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{\ast},\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
. In other words, by the
{\mathcal{T}}
–Yoneda lemma we just need to show that

5.3
Parametrised idempotent-completeness

Recall that every retraction
r:X\rightleftarrows M:i
gives rise to an idempotent self-map
i\circ r
of
X
since
(i\circ r)\circ(i\circ r)\simeq i\circ(r\circ i)\circ r\simeq i\circ r
. On the other hand, in general, not every idempotent self-map of an object in a category arises in this way, and a category is defined to be idempotent-complete if every idempotent self-map of an object arises from a retraction (cf.
[
Lur09
,
\lx@sectionsign 4.4.5
]
). We now introduce the parametrised version of this.

Definition 5.3.1
.

A
{\mathcal{T}}
–category is said to be
{\mathcal{T}}
-idempotent-complete
if it is so fibrewise. A
{\mathcal{T}}
–functor
f:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
is said to be a
{\mathcal{T}}
-idempotent-completion
if it is fibrewise an idempotent-completion (cf.
[
Lur09
, Def. 5.1.4.1]
).

Observation 5.3.2

(Consequences of fibrewise definitions)
.

Here are some facts we can immediately glean from our fibrewise definitions.

1.

We know that for
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
small,
\mathrm{Ind}_{\kappa}(\mathrm{Ind}_{\kappa}({\mathcal{C}})^{\kappa})\simeq\mathrm{Ind}_{\kappa}({\mathcal{C}})
, and so since
{\mathcal{T}}
–compactness and
{\mathcal{T}}
–Ind objects are fibrewise notions, we also get that for any small
{\mathcal{T}}
–category
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
we have
\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}\big(\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})^{\underline{\kappa}}\big)\simeq\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
. Here we have used crucially that
\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})^{\underline{\kappa}}
is really just fibrewise compact, that is, that the cocartesian lifts of the cocartesian fibration
\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}
preserve
\kappa
-compact objects. This is because
\mathrm{Ind}_{\kappa}(-)^{\kappa}
computes the idempotent-completion by
[
Lur09
, Lem. 5.4.2.4]
, which is a functor.

2.

By the same token,
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow(\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})^{\underline{\kappa}}
exhibits the
{\mathcal{T}}
–idempotent-completion of
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
for any small
{\mathcal{T}}
–category
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
.

The following result will be crucial in the proof of
6.1.2
.

Proposition 5.3.3

(
{\mathcal{T}}
–Yoneda of idempotent-complete, “
[
Lur09
, Prop. 5.3.4.18]
”)
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
be a small
{\mathcal{T}}
–idempotent-complete
{\mathcal{T}}
–category which is
\kappa
–
{\mathcal{T}}
–cocomplete. Then the
{\mathcal{T}}
–Yoneda embedding
j:\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\rightarrow\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})^{\underline{\kappa}}
has a
{\mathcal{T}}
–left adjoint.

Proof.

3.3.9
we construct the adjunction objectwise. Let

where the last is since
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is
\kappa

{\mathcal{T}}

Now
5.2.5
says that everything in
\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})
is a retract of
\kappa
-small
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits of the Yoneda image
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\subseteq\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})

\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\subseteq\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
clearly, the paragraphs above yield that

\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{C}}})^{\underline{\kappa}}\subseteq\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
as required.
∎

6
Parametrised presentability

We are now ready to formulate and prove two of the main results in this paper, namely the characterisations of
{\mathcal{T}}
–presentables in
6.1.2
and the
{\mathcal{T}}
–adjoint functor theorem,
6.2.1
. As we shall see, given all the technology that we have, the proofs for these parametrised versions will present us with no especial difficulties either because we can mimic the proofs of
[
Lur09
]
almost word-for-word, or because we can deduce them from the unparametrised versions (as in the cases of the adjoint functor theorem or the presentable Dwyer-Kan localisation
6.3.7
). In subsections
Section

6.3
and
Section

6.4
we will also develop the important construction of
localisation–cocompletions
. We will then prove the parametrised analogue of the correspondence between presentable categories and small idempotent-complete ones in
6.5.4
as well as record the various expected permanence properties for parametrised presentability in
Section

6.7
and
Section

6.6
.

6.1
Characterisations of parametrised presentability

Definition 6.1.1
.

A
{\mathcal{T}}
–category
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is
{\mathcal{T}}
–
presentable
if
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is
{\mathcal{T}}
–accessible and is
{\mathcal{T}}
–cocomplete.

We are now ready for the Lurie-Simpson-style characterisations of parametrised presentability. Note that characterisation (7) is a purely parametrised phenomenon and has no analogue in the unparametrised world. The proofs for the equivalences between the first six characterisations is exactly the arguments in
[
Lur09
]
and so the expert reader might want to jump ahead to the parts that concern point (7).

Theorem 6.1.2

(Characterisations for parametrised presentability, “
[
Lur09
, Thm. 5.5.1.1]
”)
.

Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
be a
{\mathcal{T}}
–category. Then the following are equivalent:

(1)

\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is
{\mathcal{T}}
–presentable.

(2)

\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is
{\mathcal{T}}
–accessible, and for every regular cardinal
\kappa
,
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\kappa}}
is
\kappa
–
{\mathcal{T}}
–cocomplete.

(3)

There exists a regular cardinal
\kappa
such that
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is
\kappa
–
{\mathcal{T}}
–accessible and
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\kappa}}
is
\kappa
–
{\mathcal{T}}
–cocomplete

(4)

There exists a regular cardinal
\kappa
, a small
{\mathcal{T}}
–idempotent-complete and
\kappa
–
{\mathcal{T}}
–cocomplete category
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
, and an equivalence
\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\rightarrow\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}

\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}

(5)

There exists a small
{\mathcal{T}}
–idempotent-complete category
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
such that

is a
\kappa

{\mathcal{T}}
–accessible Bousfield localisation of

\kappa

{\mathcal{T}}
–accessible, and so by

the
{\mathcal{T}}
–right adjoint is also a
\kappa
–
{\mathcal{T}}
–accessible functor and hence the Bousfield localisation preserves
\kappa
–
{\mathcal{T}}
–compacts.

(6)

\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is locally small and is
{\mathcal{T}}
–cocomplete, and there is a regular cardinal
\kappa
and a small set
{\mathcal{G}}
of T-
\kappa
-compact objects of
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
such that every
{\mathcal{T}}
–object of
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is a small
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimit of objects in
{\mathcal{G}}
.

(7)

\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
satisfies the left Beck-Chevalley condition (
3.1.8
) and there is a regular cardinal
\kappa
such that the straightening
C:{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}\longrightarrow\widehat{\mathrm{Cat}}
factors through
C:{\mathcal{T}}^{\mathrm{op}}\longrightarrow\mathrm{Pr}_{L,\kappa}
.

{\mathcal{T}}
–cocomplete for all
\tau
, this is true in particular for
\tau=\kappa
so chosen. To see (3) implies (4), note that accessibility is a fibrewise condition and so we can apply the characterisation of accessibility in
[
Lur09
, Prop. 5.4.2.2 (2)]
. To see (4) implies (5), let
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
be given by (4). We want to show that
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is a
{\mathcal{T}}
–accessible Bousfield localisation of
\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
. Consider the
{\mathcal{T}}
–Yoneda embedding (it lands in
\kappa
–
{\mathcal{T}}
–compacts by
5.1.5
)

j:\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\hookrightarrow\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})^{\underline{\kappa}}

This has a
{\mathcal{T}}
–left adjoint
\ell
by
5.3.3
. Define
L\coloneqq\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}(\ell)
and
J\coloneqq\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}(j)
, so that, since
\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}
is a fibrewise construction, we have a
{\mathcal{T}}
–adjunction by
3.5.7

L:\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}(\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})^{\underline{\kappa}})\rightleftarrows\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}:J

where
J
is
{\mathcal{T}}
–fully faithful by
5.2.1
. But then by
5.2.4
, we get
\underline{\mathrm{Ind}}_{\kappa}(\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})^{\underline{\kappa}})\simeq\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
and this completes this implication.

To see (5) implies (6), first of all
\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
is locally small and so
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}\subseteq\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
is too. Moreover, Bousfield local
{\mathcal{T}}
–subcategories always admit
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits admitted by the ambient category and so
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is
{\mathcal{T}}
–cocomplete. For the last assertion, consider the composite

\varphi:\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}\hookrightarrow\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})\xrightarrow{L}\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}

Since
\underline{\presheaf}_{{\mathcal{T}}}(\underline{{\mathcal{D}}})
is generated by
\underline{{\mathcal{D}}}
under small
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits by
3.3.6
and since
L
preserves
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits, we see that
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is generated under
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits by
\im\varphi.
To see that
\im\varphi\subseteq\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\kappa}}
, note that since by hypothesis
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
was
\kappa
–
{\mathcal{T}}
–accessible, we know from
5.2.7
that the
{\mathcal{T}}
–right adjoint of
L
is automatically
{\mathcal{T}}
–accessible, and so
L
preserves
\kappa
–
{\mathcal{T}}
–compacts, and we are done.

To see (6) implies (1), by definition, we just need to check that
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is
\kappa
–
{\mathcal{T}}
–accessible. Assumption (6) says that everything is a
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimit of
{\mathcal{T}}
–compacts, but we need to massage this to say that everything is a fibrewise
\kappa
-filtered
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimit of an essentially small subcategory - note this is where we need the assumption about
{\mathcal{G}}
and not just use all of
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\kappa}}
, the problem being that the latter is not necessarily small. Let
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\prime}\subseteq\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\kappa}}
be generated by
{\mathcal{G}}
and
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\prime}\subseteq\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\prime\prime}\subseteq\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\kappa}}
be the
\kappa
–
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimit closure of
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\prime}
: here we are using that
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\prime\prime}\subseteq\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\underline{\kappa}}
since
\kappa
–
{\mathcal{T}}
–compacts are closed under
\kappa
-small
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits
5.1.6
. Then since small
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits decompose as
\kappa
-small
{\mathcal{T}}
–colimits and fibrewise
\kappa
-filtered colimits, we get that
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
is generated by
\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}^{\prime\prime}\subseteq\underline{{\mathcal{C}}}
under
\kappa
-filtered colimits, as required.
